A real piano, right in your browser.
Play all 88 keys with your mouse, your fingers or your computer keyboard. Hold the sustain pedal, label the keys while you learn, and switch between grand piano, electric piano, organ, strings and more. Nothing to install, nothing to sign up for.
Play with your computer keyboard

Questions
Is this online piano free? Yes. Every feature is free and works without an account or a download.
Can I play the piano with my computer keyboard? Yes. The letter rows Z to M and Q to P play two octaves, the number row and the middle row add the black keys, Space works as the sustain pedal and the arrow keys change octave. You can also switch to the 61-key Virtual Piano layout in Settings.
Does it work on iPhone, iPad and Android? Yes. Tap with several fingers for chords and slide for glissando. Use the rotate button to play in landscape while holding your phone upright, or turn your device sideways for a wider keyboard. If you hear nothing on an iPhone, check that the volume is up.
Can I connect a real MIDI keyboard? Yes, in browsers that support Web MIDI, such as Chrome and Edge on desktop and Android. Open Settings, choose Connect under MIDI keyboard, and play — velocity and the sustain pedal are supported.
How many keys does the virtual piano have? It has all 88 keys of a concert grand, from A0 to C8. You can limit it to 61, 49 or 37 keys in Settings if you prefer a smaller keyboard.

title: Show HN: Twain, a diff viewer like Meld, but for the age of AI
author: andunie
body:
I love Meld, I've been using it for a while now, it's amazing how many diff viewers exist these days and how they are all awful compared to Meld.But Meld was missing some features that I thought were worth having:- all files from a Git diff shown in the same view, sequentially + a file tree on the side.
- show either the full files or only the parts that changed.
- tree-sitter-based syntax highlighting.
- the ability to comment on sets of changes and lines, and AIs can read these comments.
- the ability to search through the entire set of modified files.Twain is in Rust and based on GTK4.

title: Show HN: Things to Do API
author: invalidmonk
body: I built an api/mcp for local events: pop-ups, one-off events, concerts, etc. currently covering the SF bay area.I've been building a bunch of consumer apps lately around personalization and recommendation and have had a hard time finding this data in one spot. agents can find useful stuff through tool calls / web search, but slow.you can scrape on demand too, but i wanted a faster data set and couldn't find an existing provider for the mix of event types I was searching for.the methodology for it is to find influential accounts/posters/etc. and do a fan out across things that they co-post with.mcp: `claude mcp add --transport http thingstodo https://api.thingstodoapi.com/mcp`I'm considering adding other cities. If you're building something that needs local event data, would something like this be useful and where would you want coverage?

title: Show HN: Fakeipedia – Wikipedia for worlds that don't exist
author: darajava
body: Hi HN!Fakeipedia is an automatic world-building platform which takes an imagined world and makes a whole wiki that you can endlessly explore by clicking red links.I came up with this idea a few months ago after playing around with worldbuilding in Gemini, but I didn't want to release it until a powerful enough model could do it justice, and I decided that Argon is creative enough to write articles that are worth reading. I was surprised how well it turned out and how engaging some of the writing actually is.If you want to generate an article there is a nominal charge attached ($0.90), which helps cover AI/Stripe costs, and I think I just about break even. You can also steer the generation ala choose-your-own-adventure books when generating a new article. Everything generated is free and public for everyone to see.I hope you like it and I'm very much open to hearing about new world ideas/features that would make this project better.

title: Show HN: Pomoflow – a 1-bit Pomodoro with a todo list that syncs without sign-up
author: rochansinha
body: Pomoflow is (yet another) Pomodoro app in a 1-bit style inspired by the early Macintosh GUI. It also has a todo list you can sync between your devices without having to login to an account. A jukebox loads and plays your favourite YouTube playlists. And there are bonus weekly focus stats for the numberphiles among us.I built this because I wanted three things in one place: a pomodoro timer that looks good, a task list that syncs across my devices without an account (the apps I tried kept putting sync behind a login or a paywall), and my YT playlists I could play without having to leave the tab.A little more detail on the no-account task list syncing- To sync tasks you generate a random 128-bit key and paste the key or scan a QR code on the other device. The pairing link carries the key in the URL fragment, so the browser never sends it to the server, and the server stores only a SHA-256 hash of it. Anyone with the key can read and edit the list. Without a key, tasks stay in the browser.

TV Explorer is a streaming player that connects to free TV channels from around the world. Use it for armchair travel, language learning, entertainment, music, comparative news, religious study, or anything else you do with TV.
What is IPTV?
IPTV (Internet Protocol Television) delivers live television channels over the internet, directly from their broadcast source. Channels are streamed on demand — just select one from the list and it begins playing immediately.
TV Explorer's channel database includes news, sports, entertainment, music, and many other categories, sourced from broadcasters in dozens of countries and languages.
Where Do Channels Come From?
TV Explorer's channel database is sourced from the IPTV open-source project on GitHub, a community-maintained collection of publicly available live TV streams from around the world.
Filtering & Search
Three dropdown menus let you narrow the channel list by Category , Country , and Language . Filters can be combined. The search field filters by channel name as you type.
Favorites & Bookmarks
The heart button in the TV controls bar opens the Favorites & Bookmarks panel. Use it to favorite channels, filter to favorites only, bookmark channels to the hotbar, or save the current filter for quick access.
A red heart means at least one option is active. Your selections are saved automatically and persist across sessions.
Column Sorting
Click any column header in the channel list to sort by that column. Click the same header again to reverse the sort direction. Sorting works alongside filters.
Is This Legal?
Every channel in TV Explorer's database is a free-to-air stream made publicly available by the broadcaster. No hacking, circumvention, or unauthorized access is involved, and no login credentials are required.
Some channels may be geographically restricted by the broadcaster, meaning they are only available to viewers in certain regions. TV Explorer does not keep a list of the channels you watch.
Your privacy
Favorites, hidden channels, and Settings stay in this browser. A Watson sign-in saves those choices with that account. That account is not sent with an ad request.
When the bar at the bottom is an ad, Google and other advertising partners use cookies to serve ads based on earlier visits to this site and other sites. The request allows personalized ads. In the European Economic Area, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland, a message asks first. Allowing it leaves the request in that ordinary state. Refusing it asks for a non-personalized ad, which still uses a cookie to limit how often an ad is shown and to count ads together.
You can turn off personalized ads in Google's ad settings . You can opt out of some other advertising cookies at About Ads and Your Online Choices .
Sharing Channels
Use the share button in the TV controls bar to copy a direct link to the channel you're watching. The link can be shared with anyone — when opened, TV Explorer launches and begins playing that channel immediately.
Multiview
Each channel row has a TV icon on the far right. Click it to add a channel to the multiview player area. Three or more channels display a large featured player plus a strip of smaller thumbnails.
Status Lights
Gray — not yet tuned. Green — played successfully. Red — failed to play. Not all channels are 24/7, so a red light does not necessarily mean the channel is permanently unavailable.
About TV Explorer
TV Explorer is a demonstration project built on the Watson Engine by David Bethune.
TV Explorer

comments.author: dtagames
comments.text: Howdy HN!I launched this IPTV app earlier this year and got some great responses here on HN:https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48325624It reaches about 2,000 people a day, but the user interface never really got beyond `geek` status and I think that hindered our uptake.Yesterday, I put up a new version with a vastly different UI to try give it a more "consumer" feel, like the big streaming apps.-- A big challenge is navigating 10,000+ channels of TV without relying heavily on a keyboard or mouse. Solved here with thumbnails and scrollable, customizable sets of buttons.-- Another challenge was information density on small screens, or even on big screens without detracting from the TV-watching experience. This version does more with information hiding, tap-to-control, and hints and affordances.-- The worst problem with live streaming TV when you don't control the source is knowing what's live vs geoblocked or offline. This version fixes that by live scanning the genre and filter you asked for in the background, surfacing channels that are known to be live and streaming openly to you right now.-- Finally, the rubber hit the road with monetization. I wanted a sponsorship model like a stadium but I spent months on personal approaches to the "right" people and got nowhere. Ad supported, free TV (or sub to remove ads) is an established biz model so maybe I just give the people what they want?I got so much great input last time, I'd love to hear your thoughts on any and all of the above!-- Is this UI better than the last one, or any good at all if it's your first time?-- Is TV Explorer something you'd enjoy yourself, or share with someone?-- Finally, how would you monetize it? Is the (test, Watson) ad bar intrusive? Would you pay to have it go away, watch with it there, or leave the site?Thank you to everyone who looks at this. I'm honored to be able to reach out to this community.-- D

title: Show HN: Gondwana, a code-first C#/.NET game engine with WebGL
author: isthimius
body: Gondwana is a 2D/2.5D game engine for C#/.NET 8 that I’ve been building over the past 16 months, using SkiaSharp for rendering. I've spent my career creating web and distributed apps and that has influenced the engine's development, so it will feel very familiar to anyone with a similar background. The engine is deliberately code-first in its implementation but still includes visual authoring tools and a custom CLI.I started creating Gondwana to host my own RTS and SNES-style games, to offload the game ideas percolating in my brain. I wanted to focus more on creating gameplay systems and was less concerned with 3D graphics. The predictability and transparency of the old Win32/GDI era were the ideal for what I was shooting for, but I also wanted something faster and more portable than GDI32. To that end, I am not trying to emulate the bigger engines.Spot! became my primary dogfooding project that I’ve since pushed up to itch.io. Getting a game to that point really helped burn away the cruft that accumulates from trying to create something like this. I was able to get Spot! to render at a consistent 120 fps on my dev machine. I experienced the absolute ecstasy of getting WebGL to cooperate with the engine cycle. And I discovered that even if Gondwana is code-first, you don’t want to hand-code platformer levels, so I added Gondwana Studio to the repository. Studio uses the same file formats that are understood by the core engine. Asset handling was beefed up, UI widgets were added for things like game HUD elements and engine diagnostics, and I fleshed out the CI/release pipeline to keep it organized.As it stands currently, Gondwana supports GPU-backed OpenGL rendering with WinForms and Avalonia hosts, and a dedicated WebGL path with Blazor. Recently a good bit of effort has been put into optimizing the rendering hot-path, reducing contention between simulation and presentation, and into making the visual tooling easy to use by people other than just me. I even was able to get itch.io deployment down to a single command in the custom CLI.The engine is still actively evolving feature-wise, but the core rendering is pretty solid right now. I expect Gondwana will remain 2D/2.5D with parallax support, so I am not trying to supplant Unity, Godot, et al. Also worth noting, Gondwana intentionally does not have an explicit ECS framework built in, although one could absolutely work well with the engine if desired.The project is MIT licensed, the source is hosted on GitHub, the packages are on NuGet, and Spot! is playable in the browser at itch.io. I will include several links in the first comment under this. I’d love to see what other hobbyists or indie game devs think of the project. Feedback on usability, as well as praise and/or criticism of the architecture would be awesome.

title: Show HN: Donut Browser, the most private anti-detect browser
author: andrewzeno
body:
Hi everyone!About 2 years ago, I began to work on Donut Browser as a tool to manage browser profiles, which over time has evolved into a proper anti-detect browser.Anti-detect browsers let you create browser profiles that look like as if you have a completely different computer. I believe Donut is the most private anti-detect browser because:
- It has no telemetry and doesn't track your browsing activity
- It spoofs your browser identity in a way that looks like a real device for every profile
- It notifies you when a website takes a snapshot of your browser identity
- It is built on top of Chromium and lets you block ads and trackers at the DNS level without relying on Manifest V2
- It lets you create unlimited profiles (the first anti-detect browser to do that)
- It supports Linux, which not all anti-detect browsers do!I use Donut as my main browser and the only other browser I have installed is Tor. If you are into privacy, it offers a lot better experience than Firefox containers or writing your own scripts to manage profiles!If anyone is going to try it, would love to hear any feedback!

title: Show HN: Sill for Android – control your Mac's windows from an Android phone
author: rahimnathwani
body: Sill (discussed here: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50112739) streams one Mac window, or the whole Desktop, to an iPhone or iPad and lets you control it by touch. It's open source, so I made an Android client for it. It's unofficial and not affiliated with Sill's author: it speaks Sill's existing protocol, so the Mac side is the stock Sill app, unchanged.Install Sill on the Mac, sideload the APK from Releases onto an Android 11+ phone on the same Wi-Fi, tap your Mac in the list that shows on your phone, then look for the 12-digit code in Sill on your Mac, and type it into the Android app.Then: tap to click, drag to scroll, hold-and-drag to select text or move windows, pinch to zoom the picture on the phone, a Draw toggle for whiteboard apps like tldraw, and a key row with Esc, Tab, Cmd/Ctrl/Option/Shift and arrows. It also works over Tailscale with Sill's Remote Access.All of the code was written by Claude Code, working from Sill's Swift source and its Python test client; I tested it on a Pixel 9 Pro XL.Not done yet: drawing the Mac's pointer, a trackpad mode, clipboard sync, and a Play Store listing (I don't have Play developer account, and new individual Play developer accounts can't publish their first app until they've tested an app with a closed test with 12 testers.)(There's also a separate Android client in draft PR #89 on Sill's repo. This one is a standalone app with an installable APK. I should have checked the issues/PRs before I asked Claude to build this...)

title: Show HN: Stoke Money – Personal finance app built around a cash flow forecast
author: _wesley
body: Hi HN,I've been through many finance tracking apps, starting with Personal Capital, then Monarch, and most recently Copilot. None of them have worked perfectly for my needs.All of these apps tend to model “cash flow” as the net sum of your transactions during a month, yet while credit card charges are reported immediately, they are typically deducted from checking (cash) accounts the following month when the bill is due. As a result, I've always had to maintain a separate spreadsheet to track my actual cash flow.These apps also have a huge focus on managing budgets, which has never been for me. My spending is rarely consistent month-to-month, so every month I'm comparing my fully justified spending against my budget, and tweaking my budget until I “pass”.So I built yet another finance tracking app. It has the usual components - accounts, transactions, categories - but the core is a cash flow projection engine, and everything else is built around it.Budgets are gone. Instead, each income/spending category is projected forward from your historical activity, but not as a flat monthly number. They land in whatever account you historically use (e.g. checking account for paychecks/rent/bills, credit/debit cards for daily spending). Credit card payments are modeled automatically based on your projected credit card balance. You can set up your own recurring transfers between accounts as well, to model savings, for example.The end result is that the app can forecast how your cash moves, and you can see in advance when any account might run low. If all of your accounts look good for the next 12 months, maybe you don't have a budgeting problem.What’s made the biggest difference for me has been the MCP integration, which I have connected to Claude (but can be connected to any AI agent of your choice). I have asked it to import historical transactions by uploading PDF account statements, categorize/tag all transactions that took place while I was on vacation, and plan transfers across my accounts to cover expected payments.I hope some people that share my frustrations will find this app useful.

comments.text: Thanks. It's an interesting time for sure. Muse also launched with Plaid integration support. I haven't tested either offering (and probably won't ever trust Meta with anything), so take these with a grain of salt:- Privacy. Stoke is a paid subscription. I’m not selling your data. Caveat: if you connect an agent over MCP, what that agent does with your data is up to you. I can't control that.- Data. The core product is the projection, and it’s only as good as the data underneath it. Plaid data is imperfect, so there’s always some cleanup to do. ChatGPT and Muse may do a decent job of recategorizing transactions and even remembering those fixes for future ones, but I think direct access to those controls (categories, rules, overrides) is a better experience than asking a chatbot.- Portability. All the questions you would ask your LLM about your finances, you can still do via the Stoke MCP, so I see it as the best of both worlds.

# Weatherdeck

Weatherdeck is a status board for machines and the work running on them (a TV or phone page fed by small pushers), not a weather app and not a monitoring or alerting system.

The Weatherdeck board on a TV-sized screen, in demo mode with the ship-deck theme. On the left an amber plate lists three calls waiting on you, each with how long it has waited. On the right a pixel-art ship and two smaller ships stand for three machines, each with a name plate. Along the bottom is the log: two waiting rows with their progress, a line counting the other lanes, and the tools status.

**What you see.** Every picture here is the demo (`weatherdeck run --demo`, with `#theme=ship-deck` on the page address). Its sources are invented and nothing in it is real.

- **Waiting on you.** The amber plate counts the calls that need a person and says how long each has waited.
- **Honest progress.** Progress shows as a percent range where the source gives one (for example 38-42%). A lane the board cannot read is counted as "can't tell" (the "+7 more" line says 1), not shown as fine.
- **A quiet source is named.** The lamp by the clock counts live sources. When one stops reporting it reads "2/3 live", and that machine's ship is drawn in fog and labelled silent.
- **One board for TV and phone.** The same page is the open sea on a wide screen and one column on a phone.

Eight frames of the demo board, one every 1.25 seconds, taken over about a minute and a half. The lamp by the clock changes from 3/3 live to 2/3 live, the ship for the machine named Cinder is drawn in fog and labelled silent, and the under-way count in the log drops from 6 to 4.

In the clip, Cinder (one of the invented sources) stops reporting. Still frame.

 

The phone page from a few minutes into the demo, cropped after the ALL FINE tile: the calls, then the problems, then that tile, which is lit only when no call or problem is open and every feed reports.

It is an at-a-glance board for work reported by many sources, meant to be left on a TV or a
phone: what is waiting on you, what is moving and how far along it honestly is, what got done, what
is next, and whether you can trust what you are looking at.

- **Any tool can leave a card.** One small JSON file in a drop directory becomes a status tile; the board only reads it (docs/ADDINS.md).
- **Any tool can feed it.** A source is anything that can send one JSON document over HTTP. Sources are discovered, never configured; machines and items appear on their own.
- **Checkable.** Every push a host receives is one line in its received log (`weatherdeck received --diff`): what each source sent and what changed on the board.
- **Honest about gaps.** A source that stops reporting stays on screen, marked silent and fogged. The board never shows stale data as fresh, and says so when a source is missing. It claims no value for itself or any tool until a number is measured (docs/honesty.md).
- **Read-only, local, tiny.** Python standard library only, one SQLite file, one plain HTML/JS/CSS page. No build step, no CDN, no telemetry, no root.
- **Runs anywhere.** The same command natively on Windows, macOS and Linux, no admin needed. Run several hosts at once; every page says which host serves it.
- **Deterministic.** No model or LLM call anywhere; the only outbound traffic is an adapter pushing to a host you name.

**What this is not.** It is not a monitoring or alerting system: it never pages anyone, and it shows only what sources push to
it. It is not a hosted service: you run it yourself, on machines you choose. And it is pre-1.0 hobby software, open-sourced
because it solved a problem the author had: details may change, and support is best effort.

## Five-minute quickstart

You need Python 3.9 to 3.14 (an older one stops at startup with a one-line message; the Microsoft Store one is fine for trying it; to run it at logon or run the
beat, see docs/runbook-windows.md). Nothing to install: run it from a source checkout or the release zip. Get the code by cloning this repository
(`git clone` it, then `cd` into the folder), or by unzipping the zip that `scripts/build-package` builds from a clone. `pip install` is not supported yet and stops with a
message saying so. Below, `weatherdeck` means `python3 bin/weatherdeck` on macOS/Linux and `bin\weatherdeck.cmd` on Windows (cmd or PowerShell).

1. **See it with synthetic data.**

   ```
   weatherdeck run --demo
   ```

 Open. Three invented sources report; one stops reporting after about
 two and a half minutes, shows late from about 2:40 and silent about three minutes after start, so you can see the offline state. Ctrl-C stops it. (`--port N` to change the port.)

2. **Run it for real.**

   ```
   weatherdeck on        # background; prints the URLs
   weatherdeck status
   weatherdeck off
   ```

 The data lives in your per-user data directory (`--data DIR` or `$WEATHERDECK_DATA` to choose another).
 On Windows, `weatherdeck startup install` also starts it at every logon, with no admin rights.

3. **Send it something.** Any tool, one POST (from the same machine, no setup needed):

   ```
   curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8787/api/ingest -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
     "schema": "lookout.feed", "schema_version": "1.0",
     "source": { "id": "my-laptop" },
     "items": [{ "id": "build", "title": "Nightly build", "state": "running" }]
   }'
   ```

 The schema id reads `lookout.feed` on purpose: it is the wire name every adapter already speaks, kept unchanged
 when the product was renamed (see docs/feed-spec.md, "Schema ids").

 To feed it continuously, run the example adapter, which turns a hand-edited list plus this
 machine's vitals into a feed and pushes it to every host in a list:

   ```
   cp examples/adapter/work.example.json work.json
   cp examples/adapter/sinks.example.txt sinks.txt     # edit the hosts
   python3 examples/adapter/push_example.py --work work.json --sinks sinks.txt
   ```

 To feed it from your own tool, see docs/adapters.md, "Write a pusher for your tool".

4. **Let other devices see it.** Add addresses to `hosts.bind` in your config file (a LAN address, a
 VPN range, or both), create a token per source
 (`weatherdeck token new my-laptop`), and open the page from your phone. Once any token
 exists, pushes need `Authorization: Bearer `. For a TV, open the page full-screen on any
 machine that can reach the host, or in kiosk mode on the host itself.

 The config file is ` /config.json`, in the data directory from step 2 (`weatherdeck status` prints that
 directory; `--config FILE` or `$WEATHERDECK_CONFIG` names another file). It does not exist until you create it. A minimal one:

   ```
   { "hosts": { "bind": ["localhost", "auto:192.168.1.0/24"] } }
   ```

 Restart the host after editing it (`weatherdeck restart`). Every key is in docs/hosting.md.

5. **Remove it.** Stop the host with `weatherdeck off`, then delete the folder you unpacked or cloned and the data directory
 (where `weatherdeck status` says it is). On Windows, run `weatherdeck startup remove` first if you ran `startup install`.
 Nothing else is installed: no service, no registry entry, no files elsewhere.

## Support

| | Windows 11 | macOS (Apple Silicon) | Linux (Ubuntu, WSL2) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Host (`weatherdeck run`, `on`, `ingest`) | supported | supported | supported |
| Python | 3.9 to 3.14 (3.8 is not supported) | 3.9 to 3.14 (3.8 is not supported) | 3.9 to 3.14 (3.8 is not supported) |
| Test suite on GitHub's hosted runners (2026-10-16; 453 tests, `.github/workflows/test.yml`, run by hand) | passes on Python 3.9 to 3.14. The first run the same morning failed 13 tests on every Windows leg (nine started Node with a command line Windows refuses as too long; the rest were tests assuming a Linux machine, a code-page decode, and a scratch clone Windows would not delete); they were fixed and the second run passed all 18 jobs | passes on Python 3.9 to 3.14 | passes on Python 3.9 to 3.14 |
| Page: Chrome, Edge | supported | supported | supported |
| Page: Safari (macOS), iPhone | headless WebKit (layout, overflow, console errors); the dashboard depth scene was checked and signed off on Safari, iPhone and a 4K TV on 2026-10-10 by the maintainer, and nothing else on those devices has been (docs/device-checklist.md) | same | same |
| Page: Firefox | expected to work, not checked each release | | |
| Since you last looked (browser storage) | per browser; a browser that blocks site data shows no since plate | same | same |
| Feed schema read | 1.0 to 1.11 | 1.0 to 1.11 | 1.0 to 1.11 |
| One ship per machine (0.4.0) | TV: up to six ships, then a convoy; phone: the convoy strip scrolls inside itself | same | same |
| The open sea (0.4.1) | TV (ship deck): with nothing waiting, one banner line and the sea across the whole upper area; checked at 1920 x 1080 and 3840 x 2160 | same | same |
| Versions per machine (0.5.0) | reporter rows, the watch strip, the trust line and the phone's SOFTWARE section say each source's adapter, or "version unknown"; only a gap that changes meaning is flagged | same | same |
| Last seen and the replay key (0.4.1) | per browser tab (session storage); a tab that blocks it starts with "not yet on this screen" | same | same |
| Slowed on purpose (0.7.0) | words only (trust line, Crow's nest); nothing to check beyond reading them | same | same |

The hosted runs are the first runs of the test suite on macOS and Windows images; before them it had been run on Linux and WSL2 and on one Windows 11 PC and one Mac by the maintainer. The hosted Windows image is Windows Server, not Windows 11, and the suite runs the page-script tests with Node; the maintainer's own Windows 11 PC runs the host day to day, which the hosted run does not cover.

What each release was actually run on is in CHANGELOG.md, with the checks only a person can make
(a real Safari, iPhone and TV; only the dashboard depth scene has been signed off so far, see
docs/device-checklist.md) listed as such. Tests: `python3 -m unittest discover -s tests` (see CONTRIBUTING.md).

## Documents

- docs/honesty.md: the honesty contract on one page: what the board never does (green when silent, zero for unknown, a made-up event), where every number, creature and light comes from in the feed, the machine-alert debounce (two feeds to raise, two to clear, one keepalive of latency), and why no value number is shown until it is measured.
- docs/ledger-spec.md: the tool value ledger: one append-only file per tool, unknown written as unknown with its reason, the honest verbs (surfaced, refused, placed, landed, not dispatched), and the reading rule that turns fourteen days of lines into KEEP, QUIET, CUT-CANDIDATE or UNMEASURED. No value number is shown until it is measured.
- docs/feed-spec.md: the feed schema (1.11), how sources merge, the five lane classes, machine rest and strain, lane state (one word and one sentence per lane), goals (the goal each lane serves, with a count under it), allowance chips, black holes (no agent at the work, outside waits, queues, coming up, the shipping gap, freshness, burn rate), the library (one honest age and word per mirrored folder), the view at a glance (since you last looked, grouping by project), and what silence looks like.
- CHANGELOG.md: what changed in each release, and what it was checked on; docs/device-checklist.md: what only a person can check on a real Mac, iPhone and TV.
- docs/ADDINS.md: the card contract: one small JSON file per tool in a drop directory, shown as a tile with a stale mark. Nothing is run or imported.
- docs/adapters.md: write a pusher for your tool: what to send, the sinks file, the honesty rules for adapters, and how to test one by recording and replaying the files it reads.
- docs/hosting.md: the `weatherdeck` command, binding and profiles, every config key, transports, pushing to several hosts.
- docs/runbook-windows.md and docs/runbook-macos.md: half a page each to run a host.
- docs/runbook-feed-gap.md: a silent feed versus a machine that is down: the read-only checks in order (uptime, lingering, timers, the journal or cron log, the beat's age) for Linux, macOS and Windows, what each answer means, and whether `KillMode=process` matters for a pusher package.
- docs/beat.md: the machine beat (`bin/weatherdeck-beat`): memory pressure, swap rate, run queue and disk per machine, its cost, and how it reaches the board.
- In the source repository: `scripts/build-package` builds the distributable zip (the product only; every entry carries the commit time of HEAD, or `SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH` when set, so the same commit built with the same Python and zlib on the same OS gives byte-identical zips and `sha256sum` is a real comparison there; across machines or OSes compare per-file content instead, in a scratch directory: `unzip -q -d x && (cd x && find . -type f | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs shasum -a 256 | shasum -a 256)`, which works on Linux and macOS; file modes still differ on a Windows checkout; a build from a tree that is not a git checkout stamps 1980-01-01, so compare only builds of the same commit or of the same kind of tree), `scripts/self-audit` scans for secrets and names before a release, `scripts/release-scan` runs it and also scans the whole git history for names, e-mail addresses, home paths and tokens (see CONTRIBUTING.md). Packages that bundle an adapter for a specific tool are built from that adapter's own repository, not here.
- `examples/`: the synthetic demo feeds, a tiny generic adapter and an example host config (`examples/host/`).

## Try it without installing

Open the static demo: a folder of plain files that shows the board with a recorded feed of invented sources, no server and no
Python needed to look at it. It is built in the source repository, not from this package (which does not carry the build scripts): there,
`python3 scripts/build-static-demo` writes `dist/static-demo/`; open `dist/static-demo/index.html` in a browser, or put that folder on any static host. A yellow bar, **DEMO: recorded synthetic feed**,
stays on the screen and says nothing is live. The page replays three recorded frames in order, a slow step every 25 seconds, so
the calls, lanes and weather change as they did in the recording (with reduced motion it holds one frame and offers a button for
the next). To record the frames again, in the source repository, `python3 scripts/record-demo-feed`.

## What is on the screen

On a TV, a desk screen or a laptop (any window 700 CSS px or wider) the front door is the open sea (`#/sea`, or no route): the
fleet on the water at full screen, one ship per machine with its name plate, the headline card for the calls on the left and the
log along the bottom, on a 640 x 360 art-pixel stage. Each ship plate carries a quiet badge: how many asks wait on you from
that machine, and how many of its lanes are off course or alerting. A ship opens its plan, a place opens its list. The
**Lists** door beside the `?` (and in a ship's plan bar) opens the page board (`#/board`,
docs/theme-spec.md section 24): a header with the way back to the sea and the key, a three-state strip (needs you, needs
attention, all fine), the lanes grouped under the goal they serve, else by project (a state word and icon, the job, one
sentence, the worker's own notes behind a tap) and the sea with a caption for every picture. On a phone the page board is
`#/sea` itself. The `tv` view never shows the page board: there the sea is the whole display. The list below describes the
stage's parts (one column on a phone with the `tv` view).

1. **Waiting on you** (the one amber plate): decisions, approvals, capacity and machine problems, with where to act. A critical takes over the bar instead.
2. **Trust:** a lamp by the clock says how many sources are live and how old the newest report is; a silent source is named there, its machine reads SILENT and its work keeps its state with LAST KNOWN beside it.
3. **Machines:** a pip and a word each (OK, STRUGGLING judged against the machine's own norm, a low disk, ALERT, SILENT, LOST, or ASLEEP for a machine you list in `display.may_sleep` that went quiet during quiet hours), with vitals on the default board and the phone. A machine its owner declared RESERVED, under MAINTENANCE or DRAINING is shown calmly, with its reason and until when, and its silence is not an alarm.
4. **The log:** off course first: work that needs action (failed, blocked, a call) and work running long, nothing else. Then the rest, calmer: under way, waiting (on a gate, a PR, a person, capacity or quiet hours, and until when, counted apart), no word, landed. Each row has a project chip, a plain title cut only at a whole word, one of six row words (Waiting on you, Stuck, Can't tell, Working, Waiting on someone else, Finished) and one sentence (never a raw status line or a task id; the full text is inside the opened row; see docs/theme-spec.md section 9.5) and an honest percent *range*, or its phase ("2 of 4") when the source knows the phase and not a percent; rows that do not fit fold into one "+N more" row. Its last row carries one chip per allowance account: provider, account, window, percent left and reset time, in a fixed order.
5. On the phone, below: waiting items, work under way, waiting, landed in the last 24 hours (or since your day start), up next, releases, allowance, machine vitals, sources and the last 12 hours.

6. **Click in.** Every plate is a door to its place, and every row in a place opens in full: the calls (each with the exact line to say in chat and a Copy button; the board never sends anything), the lanes with their steps and history, what is next, what landed, the machines with their stations and reporters, and the log of every push the host received. Each level is a URL (`#/ship/ /deck/bridge`), so Back, a shared link and a pinned TV work; a TV left on a deck or on the lists returns to the open sea after a minute. See docs/theme-spec.md section 16.

Quiet hours with nothing waiting show a dim resting screen on the TV; a lost host shows a plate that
counts down to the next try.

**Themes.** The core is generic; each look is a folder under `web/themes/` (`theme.name` in the
config). `default` is plain slate with system faces. `ship-deck` draws the fleet as a ship at sea in
hi-bit pixel art (machines are deck sections, work is the crew), with self-hosted OFL fonts. Each sailor stands at the
station for its lane's stage, and a few creatures carry one piece of news each: a longboat for a landing, dolphins
escorting the first one in ten minutes, gulls that leave a machine whose reporters go late, a whale for a release, slack
sails for work gone quiet, and a lighthouse for the board's own host. Each is written to the Logbook. Opt-in sound
(off by default) rings bells for a new call. See docs/theme-spec.md sections 16 and 17;
`weatherdeck run --demo --scenario sea-life` plays every one in about three minutes.

Preview any state without touching data: add `#controls=1` to the page URL and use the buttons
(late, stale, lost, host down, empty, loading, night, anchor, sky, motion, theme). `#night=1` forces
the night palette, `#theme=ship-deck` previews a theme.

## Privacy and safety

- Binds only the addresses you list; `0.0.0.0` and `::` are refused. Default: localhost only.
- No tokens: ingest from the local machine only. With tokens: per-source, and a token cannot speak for another source.
- **View profiles:** `full` at `/`, a `tv` view at `/tv/` for a screen the household can see (task titles, repo names and pull-request links, no free text about what a worker is doing), and a redacted `public` view at `/public/` (counts, group and machine names, percent only). Each has its own optional read token, and each listen address chooses which profiles it serves, so a TV on the LAN can be given the `tv` view only. `weatherdeck privacy on` turns the `tv` view into counts only until `weatherdeck privacy off`. Redaction happens on the host, never only in the browser.
- Feed text is untrusted: the page sets it with `textContent`, under a strict content security policy.

## Layout

```
bin/weatherdeck(.cmd)    the command (launchers for src/)
src/weatherdeck/         server, ingest, merge, history store, demo player
web/                 the page: index.html, theme.js, frontdoor.js, model.js, board.js, decks.js, page.js, sightings.js, livery.js, weather.js, world.js, app.js, style.css; themes/
examples/            demo feeds, a generic adapter, an example host config
docs/                spec and hosting guide
scripts/            self-audit, release-scan, merged-check, build-package, build-static-demo, record-demo-feed (source repo only)
```

## Licence, contributing and support

MIT licensed, see LICENSE. The name is "Weatherdeck" (one word); the wire schema ids keep the earlier name
(docs/feed-spec.md, "Schema ids").

- Contributing: CONTRIBUTING.md. Open an issue first for anything beyond a small fix.
- Questions and bugs: SUPPORT.md, through GitHub issues.
- Security reports: SECURITY.md, through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting, never a public issue.
- Conduct: CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md.

title: Show HN: Putaway – sorts your Mac's Downloads into the folders you have
author: yashrajpandey
body:
My Downloads folder is full of files like download (3).pdf, IMG_4821.jpg, and Untitled.docx. I already have folders for them in Documents. I never move them because I have to open each file to know what it is. Putaway does that part.It reads the start of each file on your Mac: PDF text, OCR for scans and photos, Word, Excel, CSV, and HTML. Then it picks one of the folders you already have. It never makes new folders. It shows you the plan first. Nothing moves until you click Move, and Undo puts everything back.Demo (this run uses a SubQ key, so some files are ready to move): https://github.com/devYRPauli/putaway/blob/main/docs/demo.gi...You choose the model. The default is Apple Intelligence on your Mac. It is free, and nothing leaves your Mac. You can also use your own model through any OpenAI-compatible server, such as Ollama or LM Studio. Or you can add your own SubQ or Jev API key. Those two give a probability for each folder, so Putaway moves the files they are sure about. With Apple or your own model, you confirm each file.I tested the released build on 107 files with messy names: public IRS forms, papers, receipts, photos, and spreadsheets, plus fake secret files and a partial download. There were 19 target folders, including decoy folders that apps make, such as Zoom and Adobe. Files in an acceptable folder: SubQ 88%, Jev 85%, qwen2.5 7B in Ollama 82%, Apple's on-device model 67% (of the 99 files it agreed to read). When SubQ or Jev moved a file on its own, it was right 132 of 136 times.One surprise: Apple's on-device model refused to read three blank government forms, including the IRS 1040, as unsafe content. Putaway leaves those files in place and tells you why.It never reads files with names like .env, id_rsa, or recovery-codes.txt. If a file's text looks like a private key or a token, it does not send it. It never overwrites a file, and it skips downloads that are not complete.Install (Apple Silicon, macOS 26). The install script is 33 lines, so you can read it first: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/devYRPauli/putaway/main/install.sh | bash

 brew install devyrpauli/tap/putaway

It is a Swift menu bar app and a CLI, MIT-licensed, with no dependencies. I do not pay for an Apple developer account, so the app is not notarized. The curl and brew installs do not show the Gatekeeper prompt.I want to know which files it puts in the wrong folder, and which file types it misses. Keynote, Pages, and pptx files are filed by name only for now.

title: Show HN: Camera Controls and Motion for AI Video Prompts
author: jenthoven
body:
AI Camera Controls — Kapwing

# AI Camera Controls

Where the camera sits, how much it sees and how it moves decide whether an AI clip feels directed or random. Below: interactive references for angle, movement and shot size, plus the vocabulary video models respond to. Every prompt copies with one click.

1. 1 Bind the reference
2. 2 Describe the scene
3. 3 Keep the look consistent
4. 4 Direct the camera

## Angle

Where the camera sits relative to the subject's eyeline. Same person, six heights.

Prompt Copy Eye-level shot. Camera: positioned at the subject's eye height, lens level with no tilt up or down. Framing: natural proportions, the horizon line crossing behind the subject near their eyes. Effect: neutral and honest; the viewer meets the subject as an equal. End: holds a level frame with no camera drift. Eye level — Neutral

Lens view · Eye level

Overhead High angle Eye level Hip level Low angle Worm's-eye Click a camera position

## Movement

What the camera physically does during the shot. Watch how near and far layers separate.

### Pan right Pan / Tilt

Pan right. Camera: fixed on a tripod, rotates horizontally from left to right at an even speed. Framing: the scene slides across the frame while the horizon stays level. Effect: surveys the space and leads the eye. End: stops on the subject, framed on the right third. Click to copy

### Tilt up Pan / Tilt

Tilt up. Camera: fixed in place, pivots vertically upward from the ground. Framing: starts low on the ground and rises to the subject and the sky above. Effect: a reveal that builds scale. End: holds with the horizon in the lower third. Click to copy

### Zoom in Zoom / Lens

Slow zoom in. Camera: stays in the same position; only the lens magnification changes, no dolly. Framing: everything enlarges equally, with no parallax between foreground and background. Effect: scrutiny, as if someone is watching. End: holds on a tighter frame of the subject. Click to copy

### Rack focus Zoom / Lens

Rack focus. Camera: locked-off, no movement. Framing: focus begins on the foreground object and shifts smoothly to the subject behind it as the foreground melts into blur. Effect: redirects attention. End: holds sharp focus on the subject. Click to copy

### Dolly in Dolly / Track

Dolly in. Camera: moves forward on a straight track toward the subject, smooth and steady. Framing: the subject grows from a wide shot to a medium shot while foreground objects slide out of frame. Effect: rising intimacy and focus. End: settles on the medium shot and holds. Click to copy

### Dolly out Dolly / Track

Dolly out. Camera: moves backward on a straight track away from the subject, smooth and steady. Framing: the subject shrinks as more of the environment enters the frame. Effect: isolation or release. End: holds on a wide shot. Click to copy

### Truck left Dolly / Track

Truck left. Camera: slides sideways to the left, parallel to the subject, height and angle unchanged. Framing: near objects pass quickly while distant ones barely move. Effect: parallax and depth; a lateral reveal. End: stops with the subject on the right third. Click to copy

### Clockwise orbit Physical

Clockwise orbit. Camera: circles the subject at a fixed radius, smooth and continuous, travelling clockwise. Framing: the subject pinned centre while the whole world rotates behind them. Effect: gravity and importance; a moment crowned. End: completes its arc with the subject still centred. Click to copy

### Crane up Drone / Crane

Crane up. Camera: rises vertically on a crane arm, tilting down gently to keep the subject in frame. Framing: the ground falls away and the horizon drops as the camera climbs. Effect: release and scale; an ending. End: holds high above the subject. Click to copy

### Handheld Human Camera

Handheld. Camera: operated by hand, with natural micro-shake, breathing and small reframing corrections. Framing: loosely centred on the subject, never perfectly still. Effect: urgency and documentary realism. End: settles but never locks off. Click to copy

### Dolly zoom Specials

Dolly zoom. Camera: dollies backward while the lens zooms in at the same rate. Framing: the subject stays the same size while the background stretches and looms behind them. Effect: vertigo; the ground shifting under them. End: holds on the warped perspective. Click to copy

### Whip pan Specials

Whip pan. Camera: fixed on a tripod, snaps horizontally so fast the frame smears with motion blur. Framing: leaves one view and lands abruptly on the next. Effect: energy; a transition hidden inside a move. End: lands cleanly and holds still. Click to copy

## Shot Size

How much of the subject is in frame. Nine sizes, one figure. Drag the marker along the scale.

Extreme Wide EWS

Prompt Copy Extreme wide shot. Camera: far from the subject, static. Framing: the subject a small figure within a vast landscape, occupying a tiny fraction of the frame, horizon and sky dominant. Effect: scale, isolation and a strong sense of place. End: holds the wide view steady. Extreme Wide — EWS

title: Show HN: Tinywm – a scrolling window manager for macOS, inspired by Niri
author: bbodi
body:
# bbodi/tinywm

A scrolling window manager for macOS, inspired by niri

- Stars: 3
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 3
- Open issues: 0
- License: GNU General Public License v3.0
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-14T09:11:07Z

## Languages

- Shell
- Swift

## Topics

- macos
- niri
- scrolling-window-manager
- swift
- tiling-window-manager
- window-manager

## Top Contributors

- bbodi (4 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 tinywm 

 Your windows, on an endless strip. 
A scrolling window manager for macOS. No more resizing, overlapping or hunting for windows. 

 Download the latest release 

---

Every new window opens **next to the one you're using**, on the display you're using, and
nothing else changes size.
The strip simply runs past the edge of your screen. Scroll it with one key or a swipe, and
**every window is exactly where you left it**.

tinywm is inspired by niri, the scrolling window manager for
Linux, and brings its way of working to macOS.

 
 ▶ Watch the demo with sound 

## Why you'll like it

- **Nothing jumps around.** Opening a window never squeezes the others. Your layout stays put.
- **Silky motion.** Windows glide into place with a spring, smooth even on 120 Hz screens.
- **One key does it all.** Hold **right ⌘** and use H J K L or the arrows. Your normal ⌘ shortcuts keep working.
- **Workspaces that stack.** Keep projects apart, one strip each. Flick up or down to switch.
- **See everything at once.** Press **right ⌘ + Esc** for an overview of every window, then pick one.
- **Swipe with your fingers.** Drag the strip with three fingers on the trackpad.
- **Every display gets its own strip.** Move windows between monitors with one key.
- **Your rules.** Keep calculators floating, ignore apps entirely, stop chatty apps from stealing focus, or open an app on a chosen display and workspace.
- **Plain-text config.** One small file, reloaded the moment you save it.

## Install

tinywm needs macOS 14 Sonoma or later on a Mac with Apple silicon.

1. Download `tinywm.zip` from the latest release.
2. Open the zip and drag **tinywm** into your **Applications** folder.
3. Open **tinywm**. Apple has checked and notarized it, so it opens like any other app.

To update, quit tinywm and replace the app with the new one. Your permissions and settings stay.

**Build it yourself instead** (needs Xcode or the Command Line Tools):
```sh
git clone https://github.com/bbodi/tinywm.git
cd tinywm
scripts/bundle-tinywm.sh --install
```
This puts the app in `~/Applications`.

## Get started

When tinywm first opens, a welcome window walks you through the permissions:

- **Accessibility** is required. tinywm uses it to move and resize windows.
- **Screen Recording** is optional. It is only for live window pictures while windows move.

The welcome window also checks the macOS settings that get in the way: trackpad gestures,
Stage Manager, tiling at screen edges, click wallpaper to reveal desktop, other window managers
and Open at Login. Reopen it any time from the menu-bar icon (**Welcome…**).

## The keys

Hold **right ⌘** (the "meta" key) and press:

| Key | Does |
|---|---|
| H J K L or ← ↓ ↑ → | Move between windows |
| ⇧ + the same | Move the window itself |
| U / I, ⌥↓ / ⌥↑ or Page Down / Page Up | Workspace below / above (⇧ takes the window along) |
| . / , | Next / previous display (⇧ takes the window along) |
| W A S D | The display above, left, below or right (⇧ takes the window along) |
| R | Cycle width: ⅓, ½, ⅔ |
| F / C | Full width / centre the window |
| = / − | Wider / narrower |
| [ / ] | Stack the window into its neighbour · ⇧] pops it out |
| T | Float or tile the window |
| V | Focus the floating windows, then the strip again |
| 1 – 9 | Jump to a column |
| Esc | Overview: pick a window with the arrows or Tab, then Return; Esc closes it |
| Q | Close the window |

**Drag with the mouse.** Hold the meta key and drag any window, anywhere inside it. The other
windows make room, and a slot shows exactly where it will land: between two columns, above or
below a window in a stack, or on another display. Let go to drop it there, or press Esc to
cancel. A floating window simply moves.

Prefer ⌃⌥ over right ⌘, or different keys? Change anything in the config.

## Make it yours

Choose **Edit Config…** from the menu bar icon. A few lines go a long way:

```
default-width = 0.5            # new windows take half the screen
bind focus-left = n            # remap any key

float    = com.apple.calculator, System Settings
ignore   = com.apple.finder
no-focus = Slack                # never steals focus

send space = cmd+space          # meta+Space opens your launcher
run shift+return = open -na Ghostty
focus-crosses-displays = on     # past the last column, focus moves to the next display
open-on  = Mail -> workspace 2  # an app always opens on a chosen display or workspace
```

There is more: `meta = control-option` picks ⌃⌥ as the meta key, `gap` sets the space between
windows, `width-presets` sets the widths R cycles through, `swipe-fingers = 4` switches swipes
to four fingers, and `unbind` removes a default key. The config file that tinywm creates lists
every option with a short explanation.

## Good to know

- tinywm only asks for what it needs: Accessibility to move windows, and Screen Recording
 for live window pictures. Nothing leaves your Mac.
- By default, moving windows show as live pictures, which need Screen Recording. To record
 nothing, turn off **Show Live Window Pictures (Screen Recording)** in the menu-bar icon.
 Moving windows then show as cards with the app's icon and the window's title.
- **Open at Login** is in the menu-bar icon and the welcome window. It works from the installed
 app, not from `swift run`.
- Quitting tinywm puts every window back where it was.
- tinywm remembers your layout and restores it after a restart, as long as the apps keep their
 windows open. After a reboot it matches reopened windows by app and title, as far as it can.
 Turn this off with `restore-layout = off` in the config.
- macOS can't hide single windows, so windows on other workspaces wait just off screen.
- Floating windows (meta+T, `float` rules, fixed-size windows) keep their own frame and show
 in the overview. Meta+V focuses them one after another and then returns to the strip.

## Known limitations

- **Full-screen apps** (the green button) live in their own macOS Space, outside tinywm's strip.
- **Some windows refuse to resize**, like fixed-size dialogs and a few apps. tinywm floats them.
 An app that refuses a narrow width, such as Slack, gets wider columns: tinywm learns the
 narrowest width each app takes and remembers it. Drag the window narrower to lower it again.
- **Password fields pause the meta key.** macOS blocks keyboard shortcuts from other apps while
 you type a password. Use ⌃⌥ instead if you need tinywm there.
- **Trackpad swipes clash with macOS gestures** that use the same number of fingers. The welcome
 window and the menu bar icon warn you and link to Trackpad settings.
- **Floating windows are not kept on top.** macOS keeps the active app's windows above every
 other app's, and raising another app's window can make that app take the keyboard. Meta+V
 brings a floating window up by focusing it, and the overview shows all of them.
- **macOS Spaces** aren't tracked separately. Use tinywm's own workspaces instead, and keep to
 one macOS Space per display.
- **Built for Apple silicon** and tested on macOS 14 and later. Intel Macs are untested.

## For developers

See docs/DEVELOPING.md for the architecture, tests and how to build the app.

## License

tinywm is free software under the GNU General Public License v3.0. You may use,
change and share it. If you share a changed version, you must share its source under the same
license. For a license without these terms, contact bodidev@gmail.com.

In contrast, FiftyPlusOne's forecasting model doesn't use prediction markets as inputs:> Other forecasters are increasingly using prediction markets as signals in their forecasting systems. We do not [...] There is a poisonous logical circularity in using prediction markets to update a statistical model when the statistical model is itself being factored into the prediction market. Because of these limitations, our opinion is that if you’re going to inject prediction market data into your forecasting model, you should at least let users view a version that doesn’t rely on such data.[1] https://www.economist.com/interactive/2026/us-midterms/predi...[2] https://fiftyplusone.news/[3] https://blog.fiftyplusone.news/p/2026-forecast-methodology

title: Show HN: What will you say to 1M people?
author: mgirkins
body:
The Soapbox 
 Sign in Next draw 08:00 tomorrow What would you say if you could email a million people? 
 Every morning, one subscriber is picked at random to write a single email. It goes to the whole
 list. Tomorrow, it could be you.
 Email address 
Put my name in the hat No passwords. One email a day, at most. Leave whenever you like.
How it works
 1 Join the list
 Drop your email in. We send a link to check it's really you.
2 The draw, 08:00 daily
 Each morning one subscriber is picked at random. Invite friends for extra tickets, up to 10.
3 Say your piece
 The winner writes one email. A human reads it, then it goes to everyone at 08:00 the next morning.
Bring a friend
 1 ticket for joining. +1 for every friend who joins with your link.
10 max 
The small print, in big print
 Is it anonymous?
 Yes, unless you sign your name. We never show the writer's email address.
Who sees my reply?
 The writer. They see your message and your email address. Every Broadcast says so.
What if I'm picked and don't fancy it?
 Ignore the email. No penalty, you stay in the draw.
Can people write anything?
