title: Show HN: Reelbird, an open-source Loom and Screen Studio alternative for macOS
author: bilater
body:
# btahir/reelbird

Free, open-source screen recorder for macOS. A share link the moment you stop, then auto-zoom, smooth cursor and captions under the same link. Native Swift, your own S3/R2 bucket, CLI and MCP server. A Loom and Screen Studio alternative.

- Stars: 5
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 5
- Open issues: 0
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://reelbird.app
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-10-13T04:22:38Z

## Languages

- Astro
- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Makefile
- Python
- Shell
- Swift
- TypeScript

## Topics

- auto-zoom
- captions
- cloudflare-r2
- loom-alternative
- macos
- macos-app
- mcp
- mcp-server
- metal
- product-demo
- s3
- screen-capture
- screen-recorder
- screen-recording
- screen-studio-alternative
- screencapturekit
- screencast
- swift
- swiftui
- video-recording

## Top Contributors

- btahir (180 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 
 
 
 

 Reelbird is a free, open-source screen recorder for macOS that copies a share link the moment you stop recording, then lets you polish the same take with auto-zoom, a smooth cursor and captions without changing the link. 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Website ·
 Download ·
 Compare ·
 CLI ·
 MCP ·
 Sharing setup ·
 Troubleshooting ·
 Support 
 

 
 
 

It's a native Swift app with no account, no telemetry and no Reelbird server: share links point at a storage bucket you own, such as Cloudflare R2. It includes a command-line tool and an MCP server, so coding agents can record and share demos too. You can download it, signed and notarised by Apple, or build it from source, on macOS 15 or later.

**Why not just use Loom or Screen Studio?** Loom's free plan stops each video at 5 minutes and won't let you download it; Screen Studio costs $29 a month and gives you a link only after you export. Reelbird gives you the link when you stop and the auto-zoom polish later, under the same link, for free. How it compares.

## How it works

1. **Record.** Pick a display, a window or an area, with camera, microphone and system audio if you want them. Press ⌥⇧R from any app. Press ⌥⇧M to drop a marker at a moment you want to find again.
2. **Stop.** The link is already on your clipboard. Reelbird streamed the take to your bucket while you recorded, so it plays in any browser a moment later. A small card in the bottom-left corner offers **Copy video** (an MP4 to paste into Slack, Messages or Finder), **Save** and **Edit**.
3. **Polish it later.** Open the same take. Reelbird has planned zooms on your clicks and typing, smoothed the cursor and levelled your voice. Trim, add captions, pick a background, then choose **Update link**. Everyone you sent the link to now sees the polished version.

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

## What it does

**Records what you need, as separate tracks.** A display, a window or an area, plus camera, microphone and system audio, with no virtual audio driver. Camera and audio stay on their own tracks, so you can move the camera bubble or mute system sound after recording.

**The camera goes where you put it.** Drag the camera bubble while you record and the video follows: it starts where the bubble was and glides each time you moved it. In the editor, drag it anywhere on the preview (it snaps to the edges and centre lines), pick a corner, delete single moves or keep it in one place. Circle, rounded square or a 3:4 portrait tile.

**The camera makes room for zooms.** While the screen is zoomed in, the bubble shrinks (to 70% by default) on the same curve as the zoom, and if the zoomed cursor would pass under it, it glides to the nearest free corner and back. Both can be turned off in the Camera panel.

**Camera layouts.** For any part of the video, show only the camera, the screen and camera side by side (stacked on a 9:16 canvas), or only the screen, with a short spring between layouts. Add them on the Layouts lane of the timeline (press C), or switch while you record with ⌥⇧L: bubble, camera only, screen only. The editor starts with the layouts you switched to.

**Blur what shouldn't be seen.** Press B and drag over an email, a key or a customer's name: it is blurred (or pixelated) for as long as you want, on its own bar in the Overlays lane. **Find Sensitive Info** reads the text on screen on your Mac and suggests blurs for emails, API keys and tokens, card numbers and phone numbers (plus any words you add), following the text when it scrolls; keep each one, or Keep All. Blurs are anchored to the screen, so they stay on the content through zoom, crop and any aspect, and every strength leaves text unreadable: each cell keeps one averaged colour, so what was under it can't be recovered. Nothing is uploaded to find them.

**Arrows, boxes, labels and highlights.** Draw them on the preview, pick a colour, trim them on the timeline.

**Keeps your take if the app quits.** Every track is written to disk in 2-second segments from the first frame. If Reelbird crashes or quits mid-recording, the take is recovered the next time Reelbird opens, minus at most the last two seconds.

**Warns you while it matters.** If the microphone is recording silence, capture stalls, audio drifts, the disk is filling up or uploads fall behind, you see it during the recording, not after.

**Auto-zoom and a smooth cursor.** Reelbird logs clicks, typing, scrolls and pointer movement next to the video, then plans zooms that follow them. One slider sets how much it zooms, from subtle to punchy, and you can add, move or delete zooms on the timeline. The cursor is redrawn from that log, so it glides instead of jittering, and you can resize or hide it after the fact. Preview and export use the same Metal renderer, so the export looks exactly like the preview.

**Speed up the slow parts.** Play any part at 0.25× to 8× from the speed lane (R changes the speed of the selected part). Voices keep their pitch up to 2×; faster parts are silent unless you keep their sound. **Speed Up Typing** finds stretches of typing and of waiting with nothing happening, and offers to speed them all up in one click; each one stays on the timeline to change or remove.

**Audio that sounds finished.** **Auto level** brings your voice to a steady −16 LUFS with a true-peak limiter. **Enhance voice** removes background noise and evens out your voice on your Mac, with a strength control and a blend back to the original; the raw microphone track is never changed. **Lower under voice** turns system audio down while you talk.

**Instant share links to your own bucket.** With **Share while recording** on, Reelbird uploads a 1080p stream as you record and copies the link the moment you stop. After editing, **Update link** replaces the video and keeps the URL. Setup is in docs/SHARING.md.

**Captions on your Mac.** Captions come from Apple's on-device speech recognition. Burn them into the export, or let viewers turn them on from the share page. **Cut Long Silences** removes the pauses in one go. From the command line, `reelbird suggest` writes a title and chapters with Apple's on-device model on Macs with Apple Intelligence. No API keys. Markers you drop while recording show as flags on the timeline, and **Use Markers as Chapters** turns them into the chapter list on the share page.

**Clean frames.** Backgrounds, padding, rounded corners, aspect ratios for every platform, and **Hide Browser Toolbar** to crop the tabs and bookmarks bar off a browser window.

**Exports the usual formats.** MP4 (H.264), HEVC and ProRes with hardware encoding, plus GIF.

**Works with agents.** The `reelbird` command-line tool and its MCP server let Claude Code, Codex or Cursor list screens, record a demo of the change they just made, export it and hand you the link.

**Open project format.** A recording is a `.reelbird` folder of standard MP4 files, JSON and an event log, with relative paths. Nothing is locked in. See docs/FORMAT.md.

## How it compares

| | Reelbird | Loom | Screen Studio | Cap | OpenScreen |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Price | Free | Free plan; Business $18/user/mo | $29/mo, or $9/mo billed yearly | Free for personal use; paid from $29/yr | Free |
| Free-plan limits | None | 25 videos, 5 min each, 720p | No free plan listed | Personal use, 5-min links | None |
| Open source | MIT | No | No | AGPLv3 (some parts MIT) | MIT |
| Link when you stop | Yes, to your own bucket | Yes, on Loom's cloud | After export | Yes (Instant mode) | No links |
| Auto-zoom and smooth cursor | Yes | No | Yes | Yes (Studio mode) | Yes |
| Polish an instant link later, same URL | Yes | No auto-zoom | Link comes after export | Instant and Studio are separate modes | No links |
| Download your video | Always | Business plans and up | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Comments or viewer stats | No | Yes | Yes | Viewer analytics on Pro | No links |
| Platforms | Mac | Mac, Windows, web, mobile | Mac | Mac, Windows (beta), Linux | Mac, Windows, Linux |
| Notarised download | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Checked 12 October 2026 on each vendor's own pages: Loom pricing, Loom downloads, Screen Studio, Cap pricing, OpenScreen. Loom is the better team tool and runs everywhere; Screen Studio has the more mature editor; Cap and OpenScreen run on Windows and Linux. More detail, plus CleanShot X, Tella and Screenity, at reelbird.app/compare.

## Download

**Download Reelbird 0.1.1** for Apple silicon Macs on macOS 15 or later (7.1 MB).

Unzip it, drag **Reelbird** to your Applications folder and open it. It's signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarised by Apple, so it opens like any other app, and macOS keeps your permissions across updates. The SHA-256 of each zip is listed on its release page.

## Install from source

Building it yourself takes a few minutes and needs no Xcode.

You need:

- macOS 15 or later, on Apple silicon. It also compiles for Intel Macs that run macOS 15, but it hasn't been tested on one yet.
- The Command Line Tools for Xcode 26 or later (`xcode-select --install`), which bring Swift 6.2 and the macOS 26 SDK. They install on macOS 15.6 and later. Xcode 26 works too but isn't required.

```sh
git clone https://github.com/btahir/reelbird.git
cd reelbird
make install
```

`make install` builds a release copy of the app and copies it to `/Applications`, asking first if Reelbird is already there. Then open it:

```sh
open /Applications/Reelbird.app
```

Reelbird lives in the menu bar. Look for the robin.

Some Command Line Tools installs ship a stale SwiftPM file that breaks every `Package.swift`. The scripts detect this and work around it on their own (see `scripts/env.sh`), so you don't need to do anything. Run `make` to see every target.

### Permissions on first run

The welcome tour asks for each permission in turn. You can change them later in **Settings… → Permissions** or in **System Settings → Privacy & Security**.

| Permission | Needed for |
|---|---|
| Screen & System Audio Recording | Recording the screen and system sound. Required. |
| Microphone | Your voice. |
| Camera | The camera bubble. |
| Accessibility and Input Monitoring | Optional. The keystroke overlay (**Settings… → Recording → Record keystrokes**). |
| Speech Recognition | Captions on macOS 15 only. macOS 26 and later doesn't ask. |

**Screen Recording takes effect only after Reelbird reopens.** After you turn it on, choose **Quit & Reopen** in Reelbird (or quit it from the menu bar and open it again).

### Keep permissions across rebuilds (optional)

By default the app is signed ad hoc. That signature changes with every build, so macOS forgets the Screen Recording permission each time you rebuild. If you build often, create a local signing certificate once:

```sh
scripts/dev-signing.sh
export RB_SIGN_IDENTITY="Reelbird Local Signing"   # add this to your ~/.zshrc
make install
```

The script creates a self-signed certificate named "Reelbird Local Signing" in your login keychain and does nothing if it already exists. Every build signed with it has the same identity, so the permission sticks. The first build asks whether `codesign` may use the key. Choose **Always Allow**. `scripts/dev-signing.sh --remove` deletes the certificate. It never leaves your Mac and isn't trusted for anything except signing your own builds.

## Keyboard shortcuts

These work in every app. Change them in **Settings… → General**; Reelbird refuses keys another of its shortcuts or another app already uses.

| Shortcut | Action |
|---|---|
| ⌥⇧R | New recording; while recording, stop |
| ⌥⇧P | Pause or resume |
| ⌥⇧M | Add a marker (only while recording, so the keys type normally the rest of the time) |
| ⌥⇧L | While recording with the camera: switch the camera layout (bubble, camera only, screen only) |

After you stop, the quick actions card closes by itself after about 12 seconds unless the pointer is on it; × closes it sooner. It never takes keyboard focus, so you can paste the link straight away. **Settings… → General → After recording** chooses between the card (the default), opening the editor, or nothing.

While picking what to record, Return starts and Esc closes the picker. During the countdown, Return, Space or a click skips it and Esc cancels. When selecting an area, Return records and Esc cancels.

In the editor:

| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| Space | Play or pause |
| J / K / L | Back 2 seconds / pause / play |
| ← / → | Step back or forward 1/30 second (with ⇧: one second) |
| Home / End | Jump to start or end |
| S | Split at the playhead |
| Z | Add a zoom at the playhead |
| M | Add a marker at the playhead (click a flag to jump to it, double-click to rename, right-click to delete) |
| C | Add a camera layout at the playhead (or select the one there) |
| R | Speed: 2× for the selected part (or 3 seconds from the playhead); on a speed segment, the next speed |
| B | Blur an area: drag on the preview |
| A / X / T / H | Draw an arrow, a box, a text label or a highlight |
| 1 to 9 | Zoom depth of the selected zoom, or the one under the pointer (1 = 1.25×, 9 = 3.5×) |
| 0 | Turn that zoom off without deleting it, or back on |
| I | Make that zoom instant: it cuts in and out with no animation |
| Delete | Cut the selected part, delete the selected zooms, layout, speed or overlay, or restore a cut |
| Esc | Put down the drawing tool, or clear the selection |
| ⌘C / ⌘V | Copy the selected zooms / paste them at the playhead |
| ⌘A | Select every zoom (shift-click or drag a box on the zoom lane to select some) |
| ⌘K | Command menu: search every command and setting |
| ⌘/ | Show every editor shortcut |
| ⌘1 to ⌘8 | Background, Cursor, Zoom, Camera, Canvas, Audio, Captions, Overlays |
| ⌘= / ⌘− | Zoom the timeline in or out |
| ⌘E | Export |
| ⌘Z / ⇧⌘Z | Undo / redo |

Elsewhere: ⌘N starts a new recording, ⇧⌘L opens the library, ⌘O opens a `.reelbird` project, ⇧⌘E shares or copies the link, ⇧⌘R shows the recording in Finder, ⌘⌫ moves it to the Trash, and ⌘, opens Settings.

## Command line

The `reelbird` tool ships inside the app. Put it on your `PATH`:

```sh
mkdir -p ~/.local/bin
ln -sf /Applications/Reelbird.app/Contents/Helpers/reelbird ~/.local/bin/reelbird
```

```sh
reelbird sources                               # displays, windows, microphones and cameras, with IDs
reelbird record --display 1 --duration 30      # 30 seconds of the main display
reelbird record --window 1234 --share          # a window by ID from `sources`; Ctrl-C stops
reelbird list                                  # recent recordings
reelbird edit latest --set zoom.intensity=0.7 --trim 0:05-end
reelbird edit latest --set camera.x=0.5 --set camera.y=1 --clear-camera-moves   # camera bottom centre, in one place
reelbird edit latest --speed 0:12-0:20@2       # play 12–20 s at 2× (1 = normal speed again)
reelbird speedup latest --apply                # speed up typing and idle stretches
reelbird edit latest --layout camera@0:00-0:04 --layout split@0:30-0:45         # camera layouts for parts of the video
reelbird edit latest --set camera.sizeWhileZoomed=0.6 --set camera.smartFraming=false
reelbird edit latest --set zoom.regions.auto-3.enabled=false   # turn one zoom off (ids are in `edit latest --json`)
reelbird edit latest --set zoom.regions.*.instant=true         # every zoom cuts in and out, no animation
reelbird blur latest --rect 0.1,0.2,0.3,0.05 --from 0:05 --to 0:12   # blur an area (0–1 of the screen, or pixels)
reelbird redact latest --auto                  # find emails, keys, card and phone numbers on screen (masked list)
reelbird redact latest --auto --keep-all       # ...and blur them all (or --keep ID)
reelbird annotate latest --add arrow --arrow 0.8,0.8,0.55,0.45 --from 3 --to 6
reelbird annotate latest                       # list overlays; --remove ID or --clear
reelbird export latest --format mp4 --height 1080
reelbird captions latest                       # captions.vtt, made on this Mac
reelbird enhance latest --strength medium      # clean up the voice; the raw mic is kept
reelbird markers latest                        # markers dropped while recording
reelbird markers latest --as-chapters          # make them the chapters on the share page
reelbird share latest                          # upload and print the link
reelbird share latest --polished               # render the edit, same link
reelbird help record
```

A project can be a `.reelbird` path, a name from `reelbird list`, or `latest`. Every command takes `--json` for machine-readable output and `--library DIR` to use another folder (the default is `~/Movies/Reelbird`, or `$REELBIRD_LIBRARY`).

Sharing settings made in the app are used by the CLI too. To set them from the terminal, run `reelbird config share --help`.

When you record from a terminal, macOS asks for Screen Recording permission for the terminal app (Terminal, iTerm, your editor), not for Reelbird.

## MCP server

`reelbird mcp` runs an MCP server over stdio. Agents get tools to list sources, start and stop recordings, drop and list markers (`add_marker`, `list_markers`), list and inspect projects, edit (including crop, camera placement, camera layouts and speed), blur regions, find and blur sensitive info, add and remove overlays, export, caption, enhance the voice, find silences, speed up typing, suggest chapters, and share or unshare.

**Claude Code**

```sh
claude mcp add reelbird -- /Applications/Reelbird.app/Contents/Helpers/reelbird mcp
```

**Codex**

```sh
codex mcp add reelbird -- /Applications/Reelbird.app/Contents/Helpers/reelbird mcp
```

or in `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.reelbird]
command = "/Applications/Reelbird.app/Contents/Helpers/reelbird"
args = ["mcp"]
```

**Cursor** (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`, or `.cursor/mcp.json` in a project)

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "reelbird": {
      "type": "stdio",
      "command": "/Applications/Reelbird.app/Contents/Helpers/reelbird",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}
```

Then ask: "Record a 20-second demo of the settings page you just changed and give me the share link."

Recording through an agent needs Screen Recording permission for the app that runs the agent (your terminal or editor).

## Sharing

Sharing is optional; recording, editing and exporting work without it. Reelbird has no server, so share links point at a storage bucket **you** own. When you share, Reelbird uploads a small viewer page and the video to `https:// /r/ /`, signed with your own keys. Anyone with that link can watch in a browser, and the link never changes, even after **Update link**.

Cloudflare R2 is the recommended host: no download (egress) fees, and the free tier includes 10 GB of storage. Setup takes about ten minutes, once:

1. **Create a bucket.** Cloudflare dashboard → **R2 object storage** → **Create bucket**, for example `reelbird`. (R2 asks for a payment method even on the free tier.)
2. **Give it a public URL.** Bucket → **Settings** → either **Custom Domains** → **Add** (a subdomain such as `video.example.com`, recommended), or **Public Development URL** → **Enable** for a quick `https://pub-….r2.dev` URL (rate-limited; fine for trying it out).
3. **Create an API token.** R2 → **Manage API Tokens** → **Create Account API token** with **Object Read & Write**, limited to that bucket. Copy the Access Key ID and Secret Access Key (the secret is shown once).
4. **Connect Reelbird.** Menu bar icon → **Settings…** → **Sharing**:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Endpoint | `https://<ACCOUNT_ID>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com` (account ID is on the R2 overview page) |
| Bucket | your bucket name |
| Region | `auto` |
| Access key ID / Secret access key | from step 3 |
| Public URL | your custom domain or `https://pub-….r2.dev` |

Choose **Test Connection**, which uploads a test file and reads it back through your public URL, then **Save**. The secret is kept in your macOS Keychain, and the `reelbird` CLI uses the same settings (`reelbird config share --help`).

Then turn on **Share while recording** in the picker, and the link is on your clipboard when you stop. Or share any recording later from the editor. AWS S3, Backblaze B2 and MinIO work too. The full walkthrough, costs, privacy notes and CI setup are in docs/SHARING.md.

## Troubleshooting

**Reelbird says Screen Recording is off, but the switch is on.** Quit and reopen Reelbird; the permission only applies after a restart. If it still fails, you probably rebuilt an ad-hoc signed copy, and macOS is holding the permission for the old build. Remove Reelbird from the Screen Recording list (select it, then the minus button), reopen Reelbird and allow it again. To stop this happening on every rebuild, set up local signing.

**macOS asks again every month whether Reelbird may record your screen.** That prompt comes from macOS, not Reelbird. Since macOS 15, the system asks you now and then to confirm apps that record the screen. Choose to keep allowing it.

**A Keychain prompt asks to use "app.reelbird.share".** That's your sharing secret. It appears when the CLI reads a secret the app saved, or after a rebuild changed the app's signature. Enter your login password and choose **Always Allow**. Local signing makes the answer stick across rebuilds. For CI, set `REELBIRD_S3_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` instead (see docs/SHARING.md).

**Keystrokes don't show up.** Recording key presses needs Input Monitoring as well as Accessibility. Turn on Reelbird under **System Settings → Privacy & Security → Input Monitoring** (add it with the plus button if it isn't listed), then reopen Reelbird. Keystrokes are only recorded when **Record keystrokes** is on before you start.

**Captions say they need a newer macOS.** On macOS 26 and later, captions use Apple's SpeechAnalyzer and download the language model on first use. On macOS 15 they need on-device speech recognition for your language and the Speech Recognition permission.

**The app quit while recording. Is the take lost?** Open Reelbird again. It finishes the take from the segments on disk. From the terminal, `reelbird recover PROJECT` does the same.

## Privacy

- Recordings, edits, captions and transcripts stay on your Mac, in `~/Movies/Reelbird` unless you choose another folder.
- Find Sensitive Info reads the screen with Apple's on-device text recognition. Findings stay on your Mac; the command line and MCP show only masked previews (`sk-p…F2`, `•••• 4242`).
- A link shared while recording plays that raw take until you **Update link**, so update it after adding blurs. The editor reminds you.
- Captions and titles are made on-device by Apple's frameworks. No API keys and no cloud services. (On macOS 26, macOS downloads Apple's speech model the first time you make captions.)
- Nothing is uploaded unless you share. Shares go only to the bucket you configured, signed with your own keys. The secret key lives in your macOS Keychain.
- No analytics, no telemetry, no crash reporting, no update checks. The app never contacts a Reelbird server, because there isn't one.
- The shared viewer page plays the polished MP4 directly. While a share still has only the live stream, browsers without built-in HLS (Chrome, Firefox) load the hls.js player from jsDelivr, pinned to a version and integrity-checked.

## Roadmap

- **Joining clips.** The project format can already append other takes; the editor doesn't have a UI for it yet.
- **Focus-follow zoom.** Zooms that follow the text field you're typing in. Today zooms follow clicks.
- **Titles and chapters in the app.** Available from the CLI and MCP today.
- **Windows and Linux are not planned.** Reelbird is built on Apple frameworks from top to bottom.

## How it's built

Seven Swift modules with no third-party dependencies: capture (ScreenCaptureKit, AVFoundation), render (Metal), share (S3 uploads, HLS, viewer page), AI (Speech, Foundation Models), a shared core, the app and the CLI. docs/ARCHITECTURE.md explains the recording pipeline, sharing flow and renderer. docs/FORMAT.md documents the project format.

## Contributing

Bug reports, fixes and features are welcome. CONTRIBUTING.md covers building, tests and pull requests.

## License

MIT.

## Support Reelbird

Reelbird is free and always will be. If it saves you time or a subscription, you can support the project, once or monthly. Stars, bug reports and pull requests help too.

 The Reelbird website is hosted on ShipTiffin, which puts all your apps on one server you own. It's open source too: shiptiffin/tiffin.

title: Show HN: Toolbit – 43 local-first developer utilities in one place
author: alwinaugustin
body:
Toolbit | Local-First Developer Tools, JSON Formatter & API Utilities

# Developer Workspace for JSON, JWT, API and Data Tools

Toolbit is a local-first developer workspace with 43 offline tools — JSON formatter, JWT decoder, Base64 encoder, regex tester, SQL formatter, YAML formatter, UUID generator, hash generator, cron parser, CSV to JSON converter and more. Everything runs in your browser: no uploads, no tracking, no sign-up.

## JSON, YAML & Format Tools

Beautify, minify, and validate the structured formats you read all day.

## Encoding & Token Tools

Encode, decode, and inspect Base64, URLs, JWTs, certificates, and wire formats.

## Generators

Produce identifiers, hashes, passwords, QR codes, and realistic test data.

## Converters

Move data between formats, units, colours, timestamps, and cases.

## Inspect & Compare

Test regular expressions, diff text, read git patches, and decode schedules.

## API & Command Builders

Compose HTTP requests, WebSocket sessions, cron entries, and Docker commands.

## Text & Document Tools

Clean up text, preview Markdown, work with PDFs, and do date maths.

### Runs locally

Every transformation happens in your browser with standard Web APIs. There is no backend to send your data to.

### No uploads

Files you drop in are read from disk and processed in the tab. They are never transmitted, so confidential documents stay confidential.

### Works offline

Install it once and the whole toolbox keeps working on a plane, on a locked-down network, or on an air-gapped machine.

### 40+ developer utilities

Formatters, encoders, generators, converters, and inspectors for the tasks that interrupt real work.

### Workspace mode

Open several tools as tabs, pipe output from one into the next, and keep your working set in view.

### Keyboard shortcuts

A command palette and shortcuts for everything, so you never reach for the mouse mid-thought.

## Frequently asked questions

Does Toolbit upload my files?
: Local transformations process input in your browser. HTTP and WebSocket tools send user-initiated requests. Nothing else leaves the device: there is no analytics, no tracking, and tool input and output are never uploaded.
Can I use Toolbit offline?
: Toolbit installs as a PWA in supported browsers. Cached local tools can work without a connection; network tools still require their endpoints.
Is Toolbit free?
: Yes. Every tool is free to use, there is no sign-up, no account, no paid tier, and no advertising. The project is open source under the MIT licence.
Does Toolbit support JSON?
: Yes. Toolbit includes a JSON formatter, a JSON Schema validator, a CSV to JSON converter, and YAML and XML converters that read and write JSON.
Does Toolbit track me?
: No. Toolbit has no analytics and no tracking. Tool inputs and outputs are never collected, and apart from the requests you explicitly send with the API and WebSocket tools, processing happens locally in your browser.
Is there a desktop version?
: Toolbit installs as a PWA from supported browsers on computers and mobile devices. Cached local tools are available offline.

title: Show HN: Brian2 Atlas, a Rust engine for distributed neural simulation
author: rocklee
body:
NEXT BRAIN Computational Neuroscience & NeuroAI How it works Brian2 Atlas Models Training Experiments Explore Compute Research Blog User center Brian2 Atlas · Open-source engine
 From neural equations
to distributed execution.
 An open engine for neural simulation and native training, from local machines to distributed systems.
 Keep the Brian2 modelling interface. Bring supported models to CPU, GPU, browser and MPI runtimes through a shared execution architecture.
 Get started View on GitHub 
 Read the preprint ↗ Slides · 22 -page overview ↗ 
Model to execution 01 → 04 
 01 · Describe Brian2 model Equations · clocks · events 
02 · Validate AtlasIR 
 Typed state, schedules, effects
and random-stream identities
 Independent Rust validator 
03 · Plan Execution plans Ordering · ownership · layout 
CPU GPU Browser MPI 
 04 · Execute Native training: forward + reverse plans 
Architecture Research results Get started Try it Paper & resources The architecture
 Describe the model.
Make execution explicit.
AtlasIR connects the equations you write to how a runtime schedules work, stores state and exchanges events. It makes those choices available for inspection and validation.
 01 A familiar modelling interface
 Define neurons, synapses, clocks and monitors with Brian2. Atlas adds its own execution backends while retaining the upstream modelling frontend.
 02 A shared model contract
 Represent typed state, scheduling, effects and event identities explicitly. Validate the representation before applying execution-plan transformations.
 03 Simulation and native training
 Alongside simulation, a bounded training extension provides forward and reverse execution plans with surrogate spike gradients.
CPU Reference & AOT Run with the reference engine or compile a model-specialized native executable.
GPU Apple Metal & NVIDIA CUDA Execute supported models on Apple or NVIDIA GPUs with float32 numeric mode.
Browser WebAssembly Export a supported model bundle for execution in a browser worker.
Distributed MPI Partition supported networks across ranks, with explicit ownership and event exchange.
Choose a backend for the model features and hardware you need. The backend guide documents setup and support for each path.
 From the v2 preprint
 Measured on real workloads.
Three studies illustrate execution speed, preparation memory and distributed capacity. Each links to its methods and measurement scope.
 CPU execution 5.43 × Best-measured time ratio
 0.839 s for Rust at 16 threads versus 4.555 s for Brian2 C++ at 8 threads, on the same Linux host.
 Full-connectome simulation + recording. Reported medians; both backends constrained to 16 physical cores on one socket. Section 5.3 · Figure 4 Laptop capacity 298.9 M Synapses on a 16 GB laptop
 The PD14 workload completed 10 seconds of model time for 77,169 neurons on an Apple M3 laptop.
 Recording disabled. The compared C++ preparation exceeded its controlled memory budget; this is a capacity result. Section 5.3 · Resource test Distributed capacity 24.1 B Recurrent synapses across four nodes
 A 4.13-million-neuron multi-area model completed 100.5 seconds of model time using 32 MPI ranks.
 A documented capacity configuration, with its own source snapshot, output checks and resource records. Section 5.2 · Figure 3 
 Read the story behind the results 
 Get started · v0.1.0
 Your first Atlas simulation.
Install the tagged source release, select the reference CPU engine, and run a single neuron. Atlas runs on your own machine without a Next Brain account.
 1. Install the source release
 For a Unix-like shell, with Python 3.12+, Rust/rustup and a working C/C++ compiler available. The source install builds the native simulation and training executables.
 Installation commands Copy 
 git clone --branch v0.1.0 https://github.com/RockLi/brian2-atlas.git
cd brian2-atlas
rustup toolchain install 1.98.1 --profile minimal
python -m venv .venv
. .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install . 
 Full installation guide 
 2. Run a single neuron
 Save this as first_atlas.py and run python first_atlas.py in the activated environment. The example simulates 100 ms and reports nine spikes.
 Python example Copy 
 import brian2 as b
import brian2_atlas
b.set_device("atlas", engine="reference")
group = b.NeuronGroup(
 1, "dv/dt = (1.5-v)/(10*ms) : 1",
 threshold="v>1", reset="v=0",
 method="euler", dt=0.1*b.ms,
)
spikes = b.SpikeMonitor(group)
b.Network(group, spikes).run(100*b.ms)
print(spikes.num_spikes) Expected output 9 
Continue with Source examples ↗ GPU, browser & MPI guide ↗ AtlasIR specification ↗ 
 Atlas × Next Brain
 An open engine.
A place to explore it.
 Brian2 Atlas is the engine you can install and develop with. Next Brain brings supported Atlas models into an online workflow for exploration, simulation and training.
 How the platform works 
 Browser simulation Explore an adaptive LIF population
 Inspect a compact model of threshold, reset and spike-frequency adaptation through the browser execution path.
Guided training workflow Train your first spiking network
 Follow a digit-recognition experiment through the platform's Atlas CPU training path. Running training requires an account and an available worker.
Open source · Open research
 Methods, code and evidence.
Start with the illustrated overview, read the full manuscript, or inspect the source. The reproduction materials preserve the versions and configurations behind the published experiments.
 Open-source engine 
 Explore the code
 Simulation, distributed execution and native training. Start with the source installation guide and documented backend support.
 GitHub · brian2-atlas · v0.1.0 Preprint · v2 
 Read the manuscript
 A Unified Intermediate Representation and Execution Architecture for Heterogeneous and Distributed Neural Simulation
 Zenodo · 44 pages · 10 October 2026 Research overview 
 Start with the slides
 A visual introduction to the architecture, main results and research boundaries, with a shorter path into the manuscript.
 PDF · 22 slides · CC BY 4.0 
 Manuscript and slides by Xinjun Li · Next Brain, licensed under CC BY 4.0 .
 Reproduce the work with the evidence repository , or contribute through GitHub issues .
Cite & build on the work
 Keep the source
with the result.
 Use this citation for the v2 manuscript. For software, use the repository's citation metadata and record the exact commit used. The repository also preserves the upstream Brian2 citation.
Manuscript BibTeX Copy 
 @misc{li2026atlas,
 author = {Li, Xinjun},
 title = {A Unified Intermediate Representation and Execution Architecture for Heterogeneous and Distributed Neural Simulation},
 year = {2026},
 publisher = {Zenodo},
 doi = {10.5281/zenodo.23273257},
 note = {Preprint, version v2}
} 
 A few useful details.
 How does Atlas relate to Brian2? Atlas retains Brian2's modelling interface, upstream history and attribution, and adds its own execution architecture. It is developed by Next Brain. The repository scope explains the relationship and licensing.
 What is open source, and under which licence? Original Atlas engine code uses Apache-2.0. Retained Brian2 code remains under CeCILL 2.1. The manuscript and slides use CC BY 4.0. See the licence scope for the combined checkout.
 Where should I start with GPU or distributed execution? Start with the CPU example, then follow the backend guide for your model and hardware. GPU paths require their platform toolchains; MPI requires an MPI installation and a supported model. Browser execution uses a separate bundle-export API.
 How can I contribute or reproduce a result? Use GitHub issues for questions, bugs and proposed changes. The preprint repository contains the historical experiments and reproduction materials tied to the paper's source versions.
 Develop in the open
 Bring your next model.
 Explore the source, reproduce an experiment, or help improve the engine.

title: Show HN: Termexo – one AI operating your other coding agents, on Windows
author: gemron
body:
# gemron/Termexo

 AI Workspace Control Plane

- Stars: 3
- Forks: 0
- Watchers: 3
- Open issues: 0
- Homepage: http://www.termexo.com
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-07-24T17:25:25Z

## Languages

- Batchfile
- CSS
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Rust
- SCSS
- TypeScript

## Top Contributors

- gemron (32 contributions)

---

## README

 
 
 

 Termexo 

 One window for every coding agent 

 
 English · 简体中文 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Website ·
 Download ·
 npm 
 

Termexo puts Claude Code, Codex, and the terminals around them into one recoverable Windows
workspace. Keep several agents visible at once, see immediately when one needs input or
approval, reopen yesterday's native session, and switch the Claude CLI between compatible
model providers without rebuilding your setup.

Run the complete Windows app with one command—no Termexo account or server required:

```powershell
npx termexo@latest
```

> The latest published release is **V0.3.10, the multilingual interface update**. Termexo now
> follows the Windows language automatically, can be switched manually at any time, and presents
> its workspace, terminal, session, notification, and settings workflows in seven languages.

Termexo multi-terminal grid workbench

 
 Claude Code and Codex terminals side by side in a workspace that remembers its layout. 
 

## What Works Today

 
 
 
 Four agents. One screen. 
 Open as many real PTY terminals as you need, choose which stay visible, and arrange them
 in a custom 1–6 row/column grid. Each workspace remembers its folder, tabs, layout, model,
 and theme.
 
 
 
 
 Know when an agent needs you. 
 Waiting for input, waiting for approval, completed, and failed states are distinct. A
 persistent banner, native Windows notification, and taskbar flash bring you back to the
 exact terminal that needs attention.
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Pick up yesterday's conversation. 
 Search local Claude Code and Codex sessions across projects, accounts, branches, and
 models. Termexo restores them through the CLIs' own claude --resume and
 codex resume commands while keeping native session files read-only.
 
 
 
 
 Same CLI. Different model. 
 Point Claude Code at Anthropic, DeepSeek, MiniMax, GLM, or a custom Anthropic-compatible
 endpoint. Save providers as profiles, keep API keys in Windows Credential Manager, and
 switch every Claude terminal in a workspace together.
 
 
 
 
 

Termexo is local by default: it has no account, cloud service, or required sync. Workspace
state stays in local SQLite storage, credentials stay in Windows Credential Manager, and
Claude/Codex session histories are read-only. The agent CLIs still connect to the providers
you configure under their own terms and privacy policies.

The interface is available in Simplified Chinese, English, Spanish, French, German, Japanese,
and Korean. It follows the Windows language automatically, or you can choose a language from
the main toolbar and keep that choice across restarts.

## V0.3.10 Updates

- Add Simplified Chinese, English, Spanish, French, German, Japanese, and Korean interface support.
- Follow the operating-system language by default, react to system-language changes, and fall back
 to English when the locale is not supported.
- Add a compact language picker to the main toolbar; manual selections apply immediately, persist
 across restarts, and can return to automatic system-language mode at any time.
- Localize the workspace, terminal layout, Agent status, session center, model switching, settings,
 directory picker, runtime diagnostics, in-app alerts, Windows notifications, and taskbar prompts.
- Add language-family resolution, persistence, interpolation, and document-locale tests while
 retaining the complete existing desktop UI test suite.

## V0.3.9 Updates

- Rebuild restored Claude launch commands, model profiles, credentials, provider URLs, and hook
 environments before mounting terminals; migrate legacy `MiniMax-M3[1m]` profiles to
 `MiniMax-M3` so restored MiniMax sessions no longer fall back to Claude Sonnet.
- Add Codex lifecycle hooks for prompts, tools, permissions, compaction, subagents, completion, and
 session boundaries, with accurate terminal states for new and restored sessions.
- Add persistent waiting/approval banners, Windows notifications, and taskbar attention while
 keeping completed-task feedback concise and actionable.
- Add workspace merging with terminal preservation and safe persistence.
- Improve responsive sidebar behavior, terminal refitting, grid sizing, maximized/fullscreen views,
 hidden initial Codex commands, and narrow-window usability.
- Document the repository architecture and release workflow for Claude Code contributors.

## V0.3.8 Updates

- Enable keyring's native Windows Credential Manager backend instead of its process-local mock
 backend, so MiniMax and other model-provider API keys survive new sessions and app restarts.
- Read back every credential immediately after writing it and fail the save if secure storage did
 not persist the exact secret.
- Add compile-time backend coverage and an explicit native credential-store round-trip test.
- Existing V0.3.7 users need to re-enter third-party model-provider API keys once after upgrading.

## V0.3.7 Updates

- Add safe workspace deletion and a native folder picker when creating a workspace.
- Surface waiting-input, approval, and completed terminals across every workspace through a global
 attention center and prominent notifications.
- Keep workspace terminal views mounted, stabilize xterm sizing and focus after workspace switches,
 and restore reliable mouse-wheel scrollback without selecting an unrelated pane.
- Align the animated terminal status indicator before the title and improve its running-state
 background treatment.
- Integrate Codex's native `agent-turn-complete` notification so new and resumed sessions reliably
 transition from running or thinking to completed.
- Regenerate restored Codex launch commands before terminal mounting so existing workspaces also
 receive native completion events instead of remaining in a stale running state.
- Route a missing MiniMax or other compatible-provider API key directly to the affected Profile,
 require a replacement before saving or switching, and keep the value in Windows secure storage.
- Turn each workspace color into a complete application theme, including DaisyUI surfaces, sidebars,
 dialogs, terminal background, selection, ANSI accents, and cursor.

## V0.3.6 Updates

- Verify model-profile API keys against Windows secure storage instead of trusting a stale database
 reference.
- Treat a deleted secure-storage entry as an unconfigured credential and stop preserving invalid
 references when a profile is saved.
- Replace the low-level keyring error during provider switching with an actionable localized prompt.

## V0.3.5 Updates

- Adjust terminal font size from the workspace toolbar and persist the preference between launches.
- Move CLI tabs left or right without disrupting the selected terminal or workspace order.
- Make waiting, approval, rate-limit, and completed states visually distinct in tabs, panels, and
 the Inspector; keep up to 250 Agent events and show more recent activity.
- Preserve xterm scrollback and refit terminals when hidden panes become visible, fixing terminals
 that could no longer scroll vertically.
- Start a fresh session when switching model providers, validate custom provider credentials, and
 update the MiniMax preset to `MiniMax-M3[1m]`.
- Detect Claude 429/rate-limit and timeout failures, surface actionable notices, and resolve
 managed-account sessions against the correct isolated Claude configuration directory.
- Explain that an explicit native session resume reloads its historical context, while provider
 switching deliberately avoids replaying the previous session.

## V0.3.4 Updates

- Apply the Termexo DaisyUI theme from the document root so global surfaces inherit the correct
 foreground and background colors on every supported system.
- Replace OKLCH-only critical theme tokens with equivalent hexadecimal colors and use
 `color-mix()` only as a progressive enhancement.
- Add explicit website and desktop color fallbacks to prevent black text on black backgrounds.
- Extend browser smoke coverage to verify the root theme and computed foreground/background
 contrast.

## V0.3.3 Updates

- Published the official `termexo` package with the
 complete Windows x64 desktop executable included.
- Run the desktop app directly with `npx termexo@latest`, or install the command globally with
 `npm install --global termexo@latest`.
- Kept the package practical for npm delivery: about 4.8 MB compressed and 13.6 MB installed.
- Added release-time PE validation, build-to-package SHA-256 verification, isolated installation
 tests, and direct process-launch verification.

## V0.3.2 Updates

- Create, authenticate, manage, and switch isolated Claude Code and ChatGPT/Codex accounts.
- Launch or resume Codex with a selected account and optional model while keeping native rollout files read-only.
- Scan session indexes across system and managed account homes, and preserve the originating account during recovery.
- Resize and independently collapse both sidebars; widths and visibility persist across launches.
- Remove the Google CLI entry and hide unfinished Snapshot, Tasks, and prototype Git surfaces.
- Verify toolbar alignment, menus, dialogs, toast surfaces, compact layouts, and sidebar interactions with automated browser tests.

## V0.3.0 Updates

- Keep any number of terminal tabs and choose which terminals are visible in the active layout.
- Configure and persist grid layouts from `1–6 columns × 1–6 rows`; unused rows collapse automatically.
- Maximize an individual terminal or the entire workspace, then restore with `Shift+Esc`.
- Keep the Claude Code CLI while switching model profiles between Anthropic, DeepSeek,
 MiniMax, GLM, or a custom Anthropic-compatible endpoint.
- Batch-switch Claude Code terminals in the active workspace and restart them with their existing session IDs.
- Use `--resume` when a local transcript exists and fall back to `--session-id` when it does not.

- Detect the native Codex CLI executable and report its installed version without opening a console window.
- Start Codex in a selected workspace directory through the same managed PTY used by other terminals.
- Read Codex rollout metadata from `CODEX_HOME/sessions` without modifying native JSONL files.
- Resume a Codex session by its native UUID using `codex resume`.
- Show Claude and Codex sessions together in the Agent session center while preserving Agent-specific resume options.
- Search and filter sessions by agent, health, workspace, and scope, with partial-scan error handling.
- Adjust grid rows and columns with steppers, a visual preview, dimension swapping, and live capacity feedback.
- Use the new compact circuit-line identity across the desktop app, installers, and website.

## V0.4 Development

- Create global or workspace-scoped network profiles for HTTP, HTTPS, SOCKS, and `NO_PROXY`.
- Manage npm registry, proxy, `https-proxy`, `strict-ssl`, and enterprise CA settings without rewriting the user's global npm configuration.
- Keep proxy passwords in the operating-system credential store and reject credentials embedded directly in proxy URLs.
- Test DNS/TCP reachability and apply the effective workspace-over-global profile to Claude and Codex launch environments.
- Preview and confirm one-click Claude Code/Codex installation or upgrades from their official npm packages, with exact version or dist-tag selection.
- Apply the effective network profile to npm, preflight the registry, prevent overlapping mutations, enforce a timeout, and verify CLI health after completion.
- Multiple isolated Claude/ChatGPT accounts are now available; automatic rollback,
 system-proxy discovery, and Plan quota monitoring remain planned.

## Why Termexo

AI coding tools usually run in isolated terminals and sessions. As the number of projects
grows, developers have to remember:

- which terminal belongs to which project, branch, and agent;
- which sessions are running, waiting for input, or waiting for approval;
- how to resume a specific Claude session;
- how model, endpoint, API key, and MCP configurations fit together;
- which parts of a workspace can actually be restored after an application restart.

Termexo uses the **Workspace** as its organizing unit and turns this scattered state into
a local control plane that is observable, recoverable, and extensible.

## Implemented Features

| Capability | Current implementation |
| ------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Workspace management | Create, rename, theme, manually reorder, and switch workspaces; persist paths, layouts, and terminal configuration |
| Multi-terminal workbench | Unlimited tabs, explicit pane selection, configurable 1–6 row/column grids, pane/workspace maximize, and real PTYs |
| Claude Code detection | Detect `claude.exe` / `claude.cmd`, version, and health on Windows |
| Start agent sessions | Launch Claude or Codex with a working directory, isolated login account, and Agent-specific model configuration |
| Session center | Read-only multi-account Claude/Codex discovery, search, workspace filtering, and native resume |
| Agent status tracking | Isolated hooks per terminal for thinking, tool use, approval, user input, completion, and failure states |
| Model and MCP profiles | Manage endpoints, keys, and MCP configuration; switch Claude CLI across Anthropic-compatible backends |
| Network and npm profiles | Scope HTTP/HTTPS/SOCKS and npm settings globally or per workspace, test reachability, and inject them at launch |
| Account management | Manage multiple isolated Claude and ChatGPT/Codex logins, defaults, authentication status, and launch-time choice |
| Managed CLI lifecycle | Preview, confirm, install, or upgrade official Claude Code and Codex npm packages, then verify the result |
| Local data and secrets | Store workspace/session/event data in SQLite and API keys in Windows Credential Manager |
| Browser preview | Preview the complete UI without Rust and exercise layout flows through an interactive simulated terminal |

Termexo model profiles

 
 Models, endpoints, and credential entry are managed in one place. Stored secrets are never returned to the frontend. 
 

## Design Goals

1. **Local first** — Project paths, terminals, session indexes, and configuration stay on
 the local machine by default. Termexo does not require a Termexo cloud service.
2. **Preserve native agent semantics** — Prefer native session and configuration
 mechanisms instead of pretending that a terminated process is still alive.
3. **Coordinate terminals, do not replace them** — Termexo provides the workbench,
 state, and orchestration layer. Commands still run inside real PTYs and agents.
4. **Make agent state observable** — Map agent-specific events into common running,
 thinking, input, approval, completed, and failed states.
5. **Keep security boundaries explicit** — Secrets belong in the operating-system
 credential store, not in SQLite, snapshots, hook payloads, or logs.
6. **Grow into a multi-agent architecture** — Evolve around adapters, PTY, hooks,
 snapshots, and routing boundaries so more CLIs can be added without rebuilding the core.
7. **Extend workspaces across trusted devices** — Add sharing, remote access, mobile
 approvals, and collaboration without weakening local ownership or security boundaries.

## Current Boundaries

- Claude Code and Codex both support native detection, account/model-aware launch, local session
 discovery, resume, and lifecycle-driven terminal states. Their event vocabularies are not
 identical, and compatible-provider model switching currently applies to Claude terminals.
- When the app exits, terminated operating-system processes are not “fake restored.”
 Termexo restores terminal configuration; historical Claude sessions must be resumed
 explicitly from the session center.
- Claude and Codex JSONL files are read-only. Termexo never edits, renames, or deletes them.
- Snapshot, Git, and task orchestration surfaces remain hidden until their production
 backends are implemented.
- Automatic permission approval, cross-agent session migration, and cross-agent batch
 model-switch transactions are outside the current release.

See Termexo.md for the complete product plan and
V0.2 architecture for current technical boundaries.

## Quick Start

### Run directly from npm

The npm package includes the Windows x64 desktop executable:

```powershell
npx termexo
```

Or install the command globally:

```powershell
npm install --global termexo
termexo
```

This path requires Windows 10/11, WebView2, and Node.js 18.18 or later. Building
from source uses the newer toolchain listed below.

### Requirements

- Windows 10/11;
- Node.js `^22.22.3`, `^24.15.0`, or `>=26.0.0`;
- Rust stable, Visual Studio C++ Build Tools, and WebView2 for the desktop runtime;
- a local Claude Code and/or Codex CLI installation (Termexo can also manage installation and upgrades).

### 1. Clone and install frontend dependencies

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/gemron/Termexo.git
cd Termexo
npm --prefix apps/desktop-ui install
```

### 2. Run the browser preview

```powershell
npm run dev
```

Open. Browser mode uses a simulated terminal with `help`,
`status`, `git status`, and `clear`, making it suitable for UI development and review.

### 3. Run the desktop application

```powershell
npm run tauri:dev
```

Desktop mode uses real PTYs. If Claude Code is not available on PATH, specify it:

```powershell
$env:TERMEXO_CLAUDE_PATH = "C:\path\to\claude.exe"
npm run tauri:dev
```

## How It Works

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    UI["Angular Desktop UI"]
    IPC["Tauri Commands"]
    PTY["PTY Service"]
    Adapters["Agent Adapters"]
    Hooks["Hooks / Event Pipeline"]
    DB[("SQLite")]
    Vault["Windows Credential Manager"]
    Agents["Claude Code / Codex"]

    UI <--> IPC
    IPC --> PTY
    PTY --> Agents
    IPC --> Adapters
    Adapters --> Agents
    Agents --> Hooks
    Hooks --> DB
    IPC <--> DB
    IPC --> Vault
```

- **Angular UI** — workspaces, terminal layouts, session center, settings, and Inspector.
- **Tauri Commands** — a minimal IPC boundary between the frontend and desktop core.
- **PTY Service** — creates, writes to, resizes, and closes real terminal processes.
- **Agent Adapters** — Claude/Codex installation detection, read-only session scanning, and native launch/resume.
- **Hooks Pipeline** — receives agent lifecycle events, deduplicates them, and maps common terminal states.
- **SQLite / Credential Manager** — stores structured local data and sensitive credentials separately.

## Data and Security

| Data | Storage | Policy |
| ------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------- |
| Workspaces and terminal configuration | SQLite | Local persistence |
| Claude/Codex session index | SQLite | Upserted from read-only native session files |
| Agent events | JSONL spool + SQLite | Deduplicated by `event_key` |
| Model and MCP profiles | SQLite | Plaintext API keys never enter the database |
| API keys | Windows Credential Manager | The frontend can read only `hasCredential` |
| Native agent sessions | Claude/Codex data directories | Read-only; never modified or deleted |

For compatibility with early installations, the database filename and some internal Tauri
identifiers still use a legacy name. This does not affect the Termexo product name or new
`TERMEXO_*` environment variables.

## Roadmap

| Version | Goal | Status |
| ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| V0.1 | Workspace, multi-terminal, PTY, and SQLite foundation | Complete |
| V0.2 | Claude detection, session resume, hooks, and profiles | Complete |
| V0.3 | Codex CLI adapter and unified Claude/Codex session center | Current |
| V0.4 | Account/provider control, CLI/network lifecycle, rollback, and Plan visibility | In progress |
| V0.5 | Session summaries and cross-agent migration | Planned |
| V0.6 | Multi-agent collaboration, task orchestration, and notifications | Planned |
| V0.7 | Workspace sharing, remote computers, and mobile access | Planned |
| V1.0 | Stable release, security hardening, and complete recovery UX | Planned |

## Repository Layout

```text
Termexo/
├── apps/desktop-ui/       # Angular desktop UI and browser preview
├── src-tauri/             # Rust core, PTY, agents, hooks, database, and commands
├── docs/architecture/     # Architecture notes for implemented versions
├── docs/images/           # README screenshots
└── Termexo.md             # Product design and long-term roadmap
```

## Development and Verification

```powershell
npm run build
npm test
cargo test --manifest-path src-tauri/Cargo.toml
npm --prefix apps/desktop-ui run e2e:smoke
npm run tauri:build
```

With the local development server running, regenerate the README screenshots with:

```powershell
npm run capture:readme
```

## Contributing

Use Issues to report bugs, discuss design
decisions, or propose features. Before submitting code, make sure the change fits the
current release scope and add tests for behavior changes.

## License

This repository does not currently declare an open-source license. Until one is added,
do not assume permission to copy, modify, or redistribute the project.

title: Show HN: Tennis, a local/offline context store
author: pizzuh
body:
Hi everyone! I'm Joe, and I built Tennis: a CLI that indexes and searches your context offline. You can index any files, your Chat & Claude sessions, Codex history, etc. All local and offline.I've always hated having chats siloed in Claude and not having an easy way to connect that context in other apps. Anything that exists today has a subscription and is stored on their servers, and really wanted something fast, local, and offline.How Tennis works:
* SQLite/FTS5 (keyword) + vec0 (vector)
* model2vec / potion-retrieval-32M (512-dim, 123MB). This is a flat vector table, and what helps make this work well local/offline.
* RRF (k=60) fuses BM25 keyword rank + cosine semantic rank into one scoreTennis also creates markdown files called 'cards' at indexing time. This gives you an easy, summarized, human readable format to see what Tennis has. You can edit these files (but won't change the embeddings in SQLite).You can use Tennis via API and MCP.
It's incredibly fast, and the MCP works great as a connector to different applications (ChatGPT, Claude, Opencode, etc).You can install and use it today: https://tennis.jlachance1.workers.dev/Thanks for checking this out! I would love any feedback. Thank you

author: poppylorry
body:
# busabase/busabase

Open-source database & workspace for AI agents — structured data, durable knowledge, reusable skills, runnable apps, and human review on the writes that matter. Local-first and self-hostable.

- Stars: 511
- Forks: 38
- Watchers: 511
- Open issues: 5
- License: MIT License
- Homepage: https://busabase.com
- Default branch: main
- Created: 2026-06-23T03:35:31Z

## Languages

- CSS
- Dockerfile
- HTML
- JavaScript
- Rust
- TypeScript

## Topics

- agent-workspace
- agentic-ai
- ai-agents
- airtable-alternative
- audit-trail
- claude
- codex
- database
- human-in-the-loop
- knowledge-base
- local-first
- mcp
- notion
- notion-alternative

## Top Contributors

- mr-kelly (309 contributions)
- kwp-lab (14 contributions)
- paylm (11 contributions)
- ranglang (1 contributions)
- dajiaohuang (1 contributions)

---

## README

 

 
 
 
 

 Busabase 

 The System of Record for AI Agents 

 Different agents. One shared base. 
The open-source database & workspace where Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and your own agents keep the records, docs, skills, and apps the next task builds on. 

 
 中文  · 
 日本語  · 
 한국어 
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 Quick Start  · 
 Features  · 
 Connect an Agent  · 
 Use Cases  · 
 Docs  · 
 Community 
 

 

 

 

 

> Busabase is an open-source database and workspace for AI agents — agents and people share the same structured data, docs, skills, and apps, and writes that matter become reviewed, trusted records.

Every agent session starts from zero. Your `CLAUDE.md` lives in one repo, the best output dies in a chat, and switching tools means explaining the project all over again.

Busabase keeps the agents stateless and the work durable: connect any agent, and it reads the same records, docs, skills, and apps your team and other agents already left behind — then writes its own work back, with a diff and a history.

## Quick Start

```bash
npx busabase server
```

Open **http://localhost:15419/dashboard/local** — no database, account, or config. It starts with embedded PGlite, local file storage, and a demo workspace.

Then point your agent at it. Paste into Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, or any agent that can read a URL:

```text
Read and follow the Busabase Agent Skill — it is the single source of truth:
http://localhost:15419/SETUP_SKILL.md

Follow its onboarding to connect to this workspace. Don't choose a merge policy yourself unless I ask for one — submit the change and let Busabase apply my permissions to decide whether it merges now or waits for review. Reply to me in English.
```

**Try this:** have one agent record a project's updates and conventions, then open a different agent and ask *"What changed on this project this week?"* It answers from the workspace, not from your clipboard.

 
 Docker · Desktop · global install · from source 

```bash
# Docker (Docker Hub: busabase/busabase · GHCR: ghcr.io/busabase/busabase)
docker run --rm -p 15419:15419 -v ~/.busabase/data:/data busabase/busabase

# Global install
npm i -g busabase       # then: busabase server
npx busabase-cli --help # API client for any Busabase server

# From source
pnpm install
cp apps/busabase/.env.example apps/busabase/.env
pnpm --filter busabase dev
```

**Desktop** for macOS, Windows, and Linux: **busabase.com/download** — runs locally and works offline.

Local data lives in `~/.busabase/data/` (`pgdata/` for the embedded PGlite database, `storage/` for files). Set `BUSABASE_DATA_DIR`, `PG_DATABASE_URL`, or `STORAGE_URL` to use another location, external Postgres, or S3-compatible storage. Only one process can hold the same PGlite database at a time.

 

## Features

- **One workspace for every kind of agent output** — Bases (typed records, relations, views, forms), Docs, Files, Drives, Skills, AirApps, Whiteboards, and Workflows as first-class nodes in one tree. Node types →
- **Shared skills across agents** — keep `SKILL.md` playbooks and custom prompts in the workspace. **Playbooks** collects them into one catalog every connected agent can look up before it acts.
- **Every write accounted for** — agent writes travel as Change Requests with a message, a field-level diff, an author, and history. Permissions decide whether a change merges on the spot or waits for review.
- **Apps on live data** — ask an agent to turn a Base into a dashboard, CRM, or content desk. AirApps run inside Busabase on workspace data, with a `SKILL.md` the next agent can read.
- **Bring any agent** — no built-in model, no lock-in. Agent Skill, MCP, OpenAPI, CLI, or an ACP chat session.
- **Templates** — install a whole working setup (Bases, views, docs, sample data, apps, and its agent manual) in one command.
- **Local-first and open source** — MIT, embedded database, works offline. The same engine powers Busabase Cloud.

 

| | |
| :---: | :---: |
| Structured Base for agent data | Durable agent knowledge in a Doc |
| **Database** — typed, related, queryable records | **Knowledge base** — durable docs with version history |
| Reusable agent Skill | Workspace-native AirApps |
| **Skills** — reusable instructions and supporting files | **Apps** — focused interfaces built on workspace data |
| Agent-proposed field diff | Record history and audit trail |
| **Change Requests** — see exactly what an agent changed | **History** — source, reviewer, commit, and timeline |
| Product launch Whiteboard | Lead intake Workflow |
| **Whiteboards** — visual context shared with agents | **Workflows** — processes kept beside their data |

 
 On mobile 

Review agent Change Requests and open records from the Busabase mobile app.

 
 
   
 
   
 
 

 

## Connect Your Agent

Works with **Claude Code · Codex · Cursor · Gemini CLI · OpenCode · OpenClaw · Hermes · Buda AI · n8n** — or your own process.

| Connection | Best for |
| --- | --- |
| **Agent Skill** | Coding agents and local CLIs that can follow workspace instructions |
| **MCP** | Tool-aware agents and IDEs that need typed workspace operations |
| **OpenAPI / CLI** | Apps, scripts, automations, and custom agents |
| **Agents view (ACP)** | Conversational sessions with inline tool activity and permission requests |

Guides: Claude Code · DeepSeek Harness · Bring Your Own Agent. Open **Agent Skills** in the sidebar for the MCP endpoint and OpenAPI spec of your running instance (`/api/v1/doc`). Also on Glama's MCP directory.

 
 How writes work 

```text
Agent reads workspace context
        ↓
Agent writes data, docs, skills, or app changes — always as a Change Request
        ↓
Your permissions decide: it merges on the spot, or it waits in the Inbox
        ↓
Either way the change stays inspectable, attributable, and reversible
```

A credential capped at `changeRequest` level can only propose; a single call can opt in with `autoMerge: false`; `busabase-cli install … --require-review` holds a package's content back for approval. Anything else that is allowed to write, writes — and still leaves a diff and a history behind.

 

## Use Cases

| Workspace | What agents do | What stays in Busabase |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Software delivery** | Turn feedback into tasks, write and test code, ship, start the next cycle | Feedback, tasks, specs, conventions, release notes |
| **SEO & content** | Track search trends, plan, draft the next article in a shared CMS | Keyword research, briefs, drafts, published pages |
| **CRM** | Research prospects, follow up, log every visit | Companies, contacts, visit notes, follow-ups |
| **Team memory** | Capture decisions, sources, and operating context | A knowledge base the next agent starts from |
| **Datasets** | Label examples, attach evidence, score quality | Reviewed training and evaluation data |

Start from a template — the whole app, its data, and the manual that tells an agent how to use it:

```bash
busabase-cli install https://github.com/busabase/templates/tree/main/templates/busa-crm
```

Browse busabase.com/templates and all use cases.

## How It Compares

| | Designed for | Missing when agents do the work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Airtable, Notion, Baserow, NocoDB | People editing directly | Agent-native access, shared skills and apps, a proposal boundary |
| Postgres | Applications reading and writing storage | A workspace UI, knowledge model, review loop, and provenance |
| Agent memory, vector DBs | One agent recalling context | Structured facts people can open, cite, and correct |
| **Busabase** | **People and agents building one workspace** | — |

Busabase runs on Postgres (or embedded PGlite) itself; it is the workspace on top, not a replacement for your app's database.

## Editions

| Open source / Personal Desktop | Busabase Cloud |
| --- | --- |
| MIT-licensed and free | Hosted, multi-user workspace |
| Local PGlite and file storage | Managed Postgres and object storage |
| No login, works offline | Spaces, roles, permissions, Team Insights |
| Data stays on your machine | Web and mobile access |

**Cloud Connect** links a local workspace to Busabase Cloud through an authenticated tunnel — your machine keeps the data and runs local agents. See pricing.

## Architecture

 
 
 

`apps/busabase` is the local, single-workspace Next.js shell. The workspace engine lives in `packages/busabase-core`: nodes, records, file trees, rich node types, review primitives, search, agents, and API contracts — exposed through MCP, OpenAPI, and `busabase-cli`. Cloud runs the same engine with multi-tenant identity, permissions, and hosted storage.

**Security:** the open-source server is designed for a trusted local machine or private network. Do not expose write endpoints to the public internet without authentication and a reverse proxy; use scoped credentials and Cloud Connect for remote access.

## Contributing

```bash
pnpm install
pnpm --filter busabase dev
pnpm --filter busabase typecheck
pnpm --filter busabase lint:err
```

Bug reports, ideas, docs, and pull requests are welcome in Issues and Discussions.

## Community

Website · Docs · Forum · YouTube · X · LinkedIn

If Busabase is useful to you, a ⭐ helps other agent builders find it.

 An MCP server lets agents on your Mac use sandboxes too, with screenshots and clicks in a macOS one.
New in 27.0.0 beta 5, as a Tech Preview. AI sandboxes are tested in every build,
 but commands and defaults may still change. Models run on your Mac rather than in the VM, where they get the full GPU and memory.
Read the guide
Built-in feature set
More than start and stop.
MacVisor brings desktop VM ergonomics and virtualization-platform
 controls into one native app. These features reflect the current
 beta implementation, not roadmap items.
MacVisor 27 requires macOS 27. Some features additionally depend on supported Apple Silicon hardware.
Guests

 cloud-init sets up your account and SSH keys and the guest agent, plus, when you ask, a container runtime (containerd, Docker, Podman, k3s) and your home folder at the same path

 Flexible Storage

 Integration and operations

 Bidirectional files, clipboard, and port forwarding tunnels powered by guest tools

 Autostart, metrics, task progress, and runner health 
 The mvz CLI, serial console, and headless operation 
The MacVisor Architecture
A control plane, not a window that happens to run VMs.
MacVisor separates management, clients, and VM execution. An always-running
 control plane owns orchestration and policy. The native GUI and
 mvz 
CLI act as independent clients, while every VM runs in its own isolated process.
 That same architecture works as a desktop app, a persistent local host, or a
 CLI-driven virtualization platform.
MacVisor process model
One host, independent lifecycles
Always Online
01 Separate lifecycles
 Restart the GUI, close a display, or run only the CLI without making those client lifecycles the VM lifecycle.
 02 Crash isolation
 Each VM has a dedicated runtime owner, so one runner failure does not take down every workload or the control plane.
 03 One source of truth
 GUI and CLI issue the same typed requests and receive the same state events from the service.
 04 Service recovery
 After a control-plane restart, MacVisor reconciles live runner records and removes stale processes from its registry.
One architecture, three operating modes
Use it like a desktop app or operate it like a platform.
The same VM can move between interactive and unattended workflows without
 moving to a different runtime or management stack.
Interactive
 Native desktop virtualization
Open a VM in its own Mac window with dynamic display sizing, input capture,
 clipboard, shared folders, file transfer, audio, and USB passthrough.
Best for development, OS testing, and hands-on lab work.
Persistent
 A local virtualization host
Start VMs headlessly, keep them running after windows close, enable login
 autostart, and connect services through named networks and port forwards.
Best for always-on services, clusters, and multi-VM environments.
Programmable
 CLI-driven infrastructure
Create a Linux dev VM from a cloud image in one command, open a shell
 in it, and script lifecycle, snapshots, networks, port forwards,
 autostart, and serial-console access through the bundled
 mvz CLI.
Best for repeatable environments, automation, and local CI workflows.
Platform capabilities
The operational tools around the VM matter.
MacVisor combines native Apple Silicon virtualization with the controls
 needed to build, protect, connect, and operate a local VM fleet.
01 
 Lifecycle and saved state
 Start, pause, resume, restart, shut down, power off, suspend to disk, or reopen a hidden display without changing runtime ownership.
 Interactive and headless control
 02

 Copy-on-write storage
 03 
 Cloud images, templates and storage
 Make Linux VMs from a signed catalogue of distribution cloud images, each a linked clone of a verified template set up by cloud-init; promote your own VMs into templates, use multiple storage locations, and perform warm or cold migrations.
 Repeatable environments
 04 
 Lab networking
 Reach every VM as <vm>.mvz. Build named shared-NAT or host-only segments, create 802.1Q VLAN bridges, reserve guest addresses, forward TCP/UDP ports, customise gateway services, and apply an IPv4 firewall.
 Addressed and policy-controlled segments
 05 
 Guest integration
 macOS, Linux and Windows guest agents (installed for you on cloud-image, macOS 27 and Windows VMs) carry clipboard sync, bidirectional file transfer, port tunnels, and live guest information over vsock; on macOS and Linux also mvz shell, the per-VM Docker socket, and the snapshot filesystem flush.
 No guest network dependency
 06 
 Operations and visibility
 Track VM state, CPU, memory, disk, GPU, and network activity while the service manages autostart, tasks, and runner health.
 Fleet-level awareness

comments.author: stephenchung
comments.text: OpenAI used around 10,000 agents and billions of tokens to solve Navier–Stokes, which most people cannot afford. But research should be open to everyone, not dominated by capital. So we built this platform where people around the world can each contribute a few agents, forming a large swarm or agent community to solve difficult problems together.The platform works as follows: we select a range of difficult research problems, including Millennium Prize Problems, and provide a Reddit-like forum for each problem where agents can discuss their ideas. Most importantly, agents can publish papers that accumulate into a shared scientific literature. All papers are automatically reviewed by GPT-6 Astra to check their mathematical claims. In this way, each agent can build on other agents’ work, accumulating a robust knowledge base over time.Our policy is to leave discovery credit and any prizes awarded with the contributing agents and their operators. So if your agent solves a Millennium Prize Problem and wins the prize, the money goes to you. Participating in rStation is easy; a simple prompt to an agent such as Codex or Claude Code is enough to get started! If you have unused capacity in your subscription plan, feel free to send your agent here.We also have agents working on LLM pretraining and RL-finetuning, so you can watch AI studying how to improve AI live on rStation too!I'd be interested to hear what problems people here would want to work on together.
